x: The Regulating Act of 1773 established the first Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta.
The first Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta, was established in 1774.
Sir Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta.
The Charter Act of 1813 provided for spending at least ₹1 lakh per year on the education of Indians for the first time.
The Charter Act of 1813 ended the East India Company's trade monopoly in India except for tea and trade with China.
The Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor-General of Bengal the first Governor-General of India.
Lord William Bentinck was the first Governor-General of India.
Macaulay was the first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council.
Section 87 of the Charter Act of 1833 opened Company service to Indians without discrimination based on religion, colour, or other such distinctions for the first time.
The Charter Act of 1853 separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council for the first time.
The Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competition for the Civil Services.
Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India under the Government of India Act of 1858.
The Indian Councils Act of 1909 first associated Indians with the Executive Councils of the Viceroy and Governors.
Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian Law Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
The Indian Councils Act of 1909 introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
Lord Minto was called the Father of Communal Electorate.
The Government of India Act of 1919 introduced direct elections for the first time.
The Government of India Act of 1919 made the Central Legislature bicameral for the first time.
The Government of India Act of 1919 introduced dyarchy in the provinces for the first time.
The Government of India Act of 1919 used the term responsible government for the first time.
The Government of India Act of 1935 provided for an All-India Federation for the first time.
The All-India Federation provided for by the Government of India Act of 1935 never came into existence.
The Government of India Act of 1935 introduced dyarchy at the Centre.
Dyarchy at the Centre under the Government of India Act of 1935 was never implemented.
The Government of India Act of 1935 abolished dyarchy in the provinces.
The Government of India Act of 1935 established the Federal Court.
The Federal Court was inaugurated on 1 October 1937.
Sir Maurice Gwyer was the first Chief Justice of the Federal Court.
The Government of India Act of 1935 separated Burma from India.
The Government of India Act of 1935 created Sindh as a new province.
The Government of India Act of 1935 created Orissa as a new province.
The Government of India Act of 1935 vested residuary powers in the Governor-General.
M.N. Roy first put forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly in 1934.
The Swaraj Party made the first formal demand for a Constituent Assembly at its Ranchi conference in May 1934.
The Constituent Assembly was constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.
The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on 9 December 1946.
Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha was the temporary President of the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly.
Dr. Rajendra Prasad became the first permanent elected Chairman or President of the Constituent Assembly on 11 December 1946.
Frank Anthony was the first nominated temporary Deputy Chairman of the Constituent Assembly.
H.C. Mukherjee was the first permanent Vice-President of the Constituent Assembly.
Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946.
The Objectives Resolution was moved at the fifth meeting of the first session of the Constituent Assembly.
The Constituent Assembly adopted the Objectives Resolution on 22 January 1947.
B.N. Rau prepared the first draft of the Constitution as Constitutional Advisor.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.
The Constitution fully came into force on 26 January 1950.
The Constituent Assembly had 15 women members.
The Interim Government was announced on 24 August 1946.
The Interim Government took charge on 2 September 1946.
Jawaharlal Nehru was the Vice-President of the Executive Council of the Interim Government.
R.K. Shanmukham Chetty was the first Finance Minister of independent India.
John Mathai was later mentioned by some sources as the first Finance Minister of independent India.
The Constitution of India Bill of 1895 contained the first explicit demand for Fundamental Rights.
The First Amendment Act of 1951 added the Ninth Schedule.
The First Amendment Act of 1951 added clause (4) to Article 15.
The First Amendment Act of 1951 restricted the rights under Article 19.
The First Amendment Act of 1951 added Articles 31A and 31B.
The Ninth Schedule was inserted by the First Amendment.
The First Schedule lists the States and Union Territories.
The parliamentary form of government was first introduced in Great Britain.
The presidential form of government was first formed in the USA.
Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India.
Dr. Rajendra Prasad was from Bihar.
Pratibha Patil was the first woman President of India.
Droupadi Murmu was the first tribal woman President of India.
Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President of India.
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was the first Deputy Prime Minister of India.
Indira Gandhi was the first Prime Minister who was a Rajya Sabha member at the time of appointment.
Acharya J.B. Kripalani moved the first no-confidence motion against Nehru's government.
The first no-confidence motion was moved in the Third Lok Sabha in 1963.
G.V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
G.V. Mavalankar was also the first Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly in 1925.
The first general election to the Lok Sabha was held in 1951–52.
The first session of the First Lok Sabha was held on 13 May 1952.
The first joint sitting of Parliament was held in 1961.
The first joint sitting of Parliament concerned the Dowry Prohibition Bill.
Nargis Dutt was the first actress nominated to the Rajya Sabha in 1980.
The Leader of the Opposition was first recognised in the Lok Sabha in 1969.
The Chamber of Princes had 120 members.
The Chamber of Princes was created under the Government of India Act of 1919.
Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner was the first Chancellor of the Chamber of Princes.
The Estimates Committee was constituted for the first time in 1950.
The Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee was the first such committee established by any Indian legislature.
The Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee was constituted in 1997.
The Lok Sabha Ethics Committee was first constituted in 2000.
The Public Accounts Committee was first set up in 1921.
The Public Accounts Committee was set up under the Government of India Act of 1919.
Justice M. Fathima Beevi was the first woman Judge of the Supreme Court in 1989.
Justice M. Fathima Beevi was the first Muslim woman in the higher judiciary.
The doctrine of Judicial Review was first propounded in the USA.
The doctrine of Judicial Review was first propounded in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.
The Basic Structure doctrine was first propounded in Kesavananda Bharati in 1973.
The Supreme Court first held that Fundamental Rights were amendable in the Shankari Prasad case.
The first Public Interest Litigation considered was Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar in 1979.
Sarojini Naidu was the first woman Governor of any State.
Sarojini Naidu was the Governor of Uttar Pradesh.
Sucheta Kripalani was the first woman Chief Minister of any State.
Sucheta Kripalani was the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh.
President's Rule under Article 356 was first imposed in PEPSU in 1953, according to some sources.
President's Rule under Article 356 was first imposed in Punjab in 1951, according to some sources.
The First Finance Commission was constituted in 1951, according to some sources.
The First Finance Commission was set up in 1952, according to some sources.
K.C. Neogy was the first Chairman of the Finance Commission.
Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Chairman of the Planning Commission in an ex-officio capacity.
Gulzarilal Nanda was the first Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission.
Arvind Panagariya was the first Vice-Chairman of NITI Aayog.
The Inter-State Council was first established in May or December 1990.
The institution of Ombudsman was first created in Sweden in 1809.
The First Administrative Reforms Commission was established in 1966.
The First Administrative Reforms Commission recommended the establishment of Lokpal and Lokayuktas.
Morarji Desai submitted the interim report of the First Administrative Reforms Commission on Lokpal and Lokayuktas.
The first Lokpal Bill was presented in 1968.
Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose was the first Lokpal of India.
Maharashtra was the first state to introduce a Lokayukta in 1971 or 1972.
Odisha was the first state to pass a Lokayukta Act.
Justice Ranganath Misra was the first Chairman of the National Human Rights Commission in 1993.
M.C. Setalvad was the Chairman of the First Law Commission of independent India in 1955.
The Public Service Commission was first established under the Government of India Act of 1919.
The Public Service Commission was established on 1 October 1926.
Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner.
Sukumar Sen served as Chief Election Commissioner from 1950 to 1958.
V.S. Ramadevi was the first woman Chief Election Commissioner.
The voting age was lowered to 18 by the 61st Amendment.
The voting age of 18 was first exercised in the 1989 General Election.
VVPAT was first used in the Noksen Assembly by-election in Nagaland on 4 September 2013.
Political parties received constitutional recognition for the first time in 1985.
The 52nd Amendment of 1985 provided constitutional recognition to political parties through the Tenth Schedule and anti-defection provisions.
Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee was the first President of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh.
Atal Bihari Vajpayee was the first President of the BJP in 1980.
The First Official Language Commission was established in 1955.
B.G. Kher headed the First Official Language Commission.
Tamil was declared the first Classical Language.
The first Municipal Corporation in India was established at Madras in 1688.
Panchayati Raj was first inaugurated on 2 October 1959 at Nagaur in Rajasthan.
Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur.
Rajasthan was the first state in Panchayati Raj.
Andhra Pradesh was the second state in Panchayati Raj.
Madhya Pradesh was the first state to implement the 73rd Amendment in its true spirit.
The Community Development Programme of 1952 was the first major rural development programme after independence.
The National Extension Service started in 1953.
Constitutional Development (Company Rule & Crown Rule)
• Regulating Act 1773: Established the first Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta (1774). First Chief Justice: Sir Elijah Impey.
• Charter Act 1813: First time provision made for spending at least ₹1 lakh per year on education of Indians; ended Company’s trade monopoly in India (except tea & China).

• Charter Act 1833: Made Governor-General of Bengal the first Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck). First Law Member of Governor-General’s Council → Macaulay. Section 87 first opened Company service to Indians without discrimination of religion, colour, etc.
• Charter Act 1853: First time separated legislative & executive functions of Governor- General’s Council; introduced open competition for Civil Services.
• Government of India Act 1858: Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.

• Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto): First time Indians associated with Viceroy’s & Governors’ Executive Councils. Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian Law Member of Viceroy’s Executive Council. Introduced separate electorate for Muslims (Lord Minto called “Father of Communal Electorate”).
• Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford):
o First time introduced direct elections. o First time made Central Legislature bicameral. o First time introduced dyarchy in provinces. o First time used the term “responsible government”.
• Government of India Act 1935:
o First time provided for an All-India Federation (never came into existence). o Introduced dyarchy at the Centre (never implemented) and abolished it in
provinces. o Established Federal Court (inaugurated 1 Oct 1937; first Chief Justice: Sir
Maurice Gwyer). o Separated Burma from India; created Sindh & Orissa as new provinces. o Residuary powers vested in Governor-General.
Constituent Assembly & Making of Constitution
• Idea of Constituent Assembly first put forward by M.N. Roy (1934).
• First formal demand by Swaraj Party (Ranchi conference, May 1934).
• Constituent Assembly constituted under Cabinet Mission Plan 1946.
• First meeting: 9 December 1946 (temporary President: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha).
• First permanent elected Chairman/President: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (11 Dec 1946).
• First nominated temporary Deputy Chairman: Frank Anthony.
• First permanent Vice-President: H.C. Mukherjee.
• Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946 (5th meeting of 1st session); adopted 22 January 1947.
• First draft of the Constitution prepared by Constitutional Advisor B.N. Rau.
• Constitution adopted: 26 November 1949; fully came into force: 26 January 1950.
• Number of women members in Constituent Assembly: 15.
Interim Government (1946)
• Announced: 24 August 1946; took charge: 2 September 1946.
• Vice-President of Executive Council: Jawaharlal Nehru.
• First Finance Minister of Independent India: R.K. Shanmukham Chetty (some sources also mention John Mathai later).
Fundamental Rights, Schedules, Amendments
• First explicit demand for Fundamental Rights: Constitution of India Bill, 1895.
• First Amendment Act 1951: Added 9th Schedule; added clause (4) to Art. 15; restricted Art. 19 rights; added Arts. 31A & 31B.
• Ninth Schedule inserted by First Amendment.
• First Schedule lists States & Union Territories.
• Parliamentary form of government first introduced in Great Britain.
• Presidential form first formed in USA.
President, Vice-President, Council of Ministers
• First President of India: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (from Bihar).
• First Woman President: Pratibha Patil.
• First Tribal Woman President: Droupadi Murmu.
• First Vice-President: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan.
• First Deputy Prime Minister: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
• Indira Gandhi was the first Prime Minister who was a Rajya Sabha member at the time of appointment.
• First no-confidence motion: Moved by Acharya J.B. Kripalani against Nehru’s government (3rd Lok Sabha, 1963).
Parliament
• First Speaker of Lok Sabha: G.V. Mavalankar (also first Speaker of Central Legislative Assembly in 1925).
• First Tribal Speaker of Lok Sabha: P.A. Sangma (1996).
• First General Election to Lok Sabha: 1951–52 (first session of 1st Lok Sabha: 13 May 1952).
• First joint sitting of Parliament: 1961 (Dowry Prohibition Bill).
• First actress nominated to Rajya Sabha: Nargis Dutt (1980).
• Leader of Opposition first recognised in Lok Sabha: 1969.
• Chamber of Princes (120 members) created under Act of 1919; first Chancellor: Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner.
• Estimates Committee constituted for the first time in 1950.
• Ethics Committee (Rajya Sabha) – first such committee by any Indian legislature – constituted 1997; Lok Sabha Ethics Committee first constituted 2000.
• Public Accounts Committee set up first in 1921 (under GoI Act 1919).
Judiciary
• Federal Court established under GoI Act 1935 (1 Oct 1937); first CJ: Sir Maurice Gwyer.
• First woman Judge of Supreme Court: Justice M. Fathima Beevi (1989); also first Muslim woman in higher judiciary.
• Doctrine of Judicial Review first propounded in USA (Marbury v. Madison, 1803).
• Basic Structure doctrine first propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
• Supreme Court first held Fundamental Rights amendable in Shankari Prasad case.
• First PIL considered: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979).
Governor & State Legislature
• First woman Governor of any State: Sarojini Naidu (Uttar Pradesh).
• First woman Chief Minister of any State: Sucheta Kripalani (Uttar Pradesh).
Centre-State Relations, Emergency, Finance Commission, Planning
• President’s Rule (Art. 356) first imposed: PEPSU (1953) / Punjab (1951 – sources vary slightly).
• First Finance Commission: Constituted 1951 / set up 1952 under K.C. Neogy (first Chairman).
• First Chairman of Planning Commission: Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru (ex-officio).
• First Deputy Chairman of Planning Commission: Gulzarilal Nanda.
• First Vice-Chairman of NITI Aayog: Arvind Panagariya.
• Inter-State Council first established: May/December 1990.
Lokpal, Commissions, Election Commission
• Institution of Ombudsman first created in Sweden (1809).
• First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966) recommended Lokpal & Lokayuktas (interim report by Morarji Desai).
• First Lokpal Bill presented: 1968.
• First Lokpal of India: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose.
• Maharashtra – first state to introduce Lokayukta (1971/1972). Odisha – first to pass Lokayukta Act.
• First Chairman of National Human Rights Commission: Justice Ranganath Misra (1993).
• First Law Commission of Independent India (1955): Chairman M.C. Setalvad.
• Public Service Commission first established under GoI Act 1919 (1 Oct 1926).
• First Chief Election Commissioner: Sukumar Sen (1950–1958).
• First woman Chief Election Commissioner: V.S. Ramadevi.
• Voting age lowered to 18 by 61st Amendment; first exercised in 1989 General Election.
• VVPAT first used: Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland (4 Sept 2013).
Political Parties, Official Language, Panchayati Raj
• Political parties got constitutional recognition for the first time: 1985 (52nd Amendment – 10th Schedule / Anti-defection).
• First President of Bharatiya Jana Sangh: Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee.
• First President of BJP: Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1980).
• First Official Language Commission: 1955 under B.G. Kher.
• Tamil declared first Classical Language.
• First Municipal Corporation in India: Madras (1688).
• Panchayati Raj first inaugurated: 2 October 1959 in Nagaur (Rajasthan) by Nehru. Rajasthan first state; Andhra Pradesh second.
• Madhya Pradesh – first state to implement 73rd Amendment in true spirit.
• Community Development Programme (1952) was the first major rural development programme after independence; National Extension Service started 1953.

Judicial review was borrowed from the USA.
The independence of the judiciary was borrowed from the USA.
The idea of the Preamble was borrowed from the USA.
The post of Vice-President was borrowed from the USA.
The impeachment of the President was borrowed from the USA.
The removal of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts was borrowed from the USA.
The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from Ireland.
The method of election of the President was borrowed from Ireland.
The nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha was borrowed from Ireland.
The federation with a strong Centre was borrowed from Canada.
The residuary powers with the Centre were borrowed from Canada.
The appointment of Governors by the Centre was borrowed from Canada.
The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court was borrowed from Canada.
The Concurrent List was borrowed from Australia.
The joint sitting of both Houses was borrowed from Australia.
The freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse was borrowed from Australia.
The language of the Preamble was borrowed from Australia.
The Emergency Provisions, except the Financial Emergency, were borrowed from Germany’s Weimar Constitution.
The procedure established by law was borrowed from Japan.
The procedure for constitutional amendment was borrowed from South Africa.
The election of members of the Rajya Sabha was borrowed from South Africa.
The Fundamental Duties were borrowed from the USSR.
The ideals of social, economic and political justice in the Preamble were borrowed from the USSR.
The ideal of a republic was borrowed from France.
The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble were borrowed from France.
The Government of India Act, 1935 provided the structural and administrative backbone.
The federal scheme was associated with the Government of India Act, 1935.
The Governor was associated with the Government of India Act, 1935.
The judiciary was associated with the Government of India Act, 1935.
Emergency provisions were associated with the Government of India Act, 1935.
The Public Service Commission was associated with the Government of India Act, 1935.

President
Constitutional Position
• Article 52: There shall be a President of India.
• Article 53: Executive power of the Union is vested in the President (exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to him).
• Nominal / Constitutional Head of the State (Real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister).
• First Citizen of India and symbol of unity, integrity and solidarity of the nation.
• Supreme Commander of the Defence Forces (Art. 53(2)).
Election (Art. 54 & 55)
• Indirect election by an Electoral College consisting of:
o Elected members of both Houses of Parliament o Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States o Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the Union Territories of Delhi
and Puducherry (added by 70th Amendment)
• Nominated members of Parliament and State Legislative Councils do not participate.
• System of Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote + Secret Ballot.
• Value of vote of MLA and MP is calculated to ensure uniformity among states and parity between Union and States.
• Disputes regarding election decided by the Supreme Court (final).
Qualifications (Art. 58)
1\. Citizen of India 2. Completed 35 years of age 3. Qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha 4. Does not hold any office of profit
Term, Resignation & Removal
• Term: 5 years (Art. 56)
• Eligible for re-election any number of times (Art. 57)
• Resignation addressed to the Vice-President
• Can be removed by Impeachment for violation of the Constitution (Art. 61)
o Charge can be preferred by either House o Special majority required in both Houses
o Only elected members of State Assemblies do not participate in impeachment
(they do vote in election)
Vacancy
• In case of death, resignation, removal or otherwise → Vice-President acts as President (Art. 65)
• If both offices vacant → Chief Jus ce of India (or senior-most Judge of SC) acts as President (President’s Succession Act)
Powers of the President
1\. Executive Powers
• Appoints: Prime Minister, other Ministers, Governors, Judges of SC & HC, CAG, Attorney General, UPSC Chairman & members, Election Commissioners, Finance Commission, etc.
• Appoints the Prime Minister (normally leader of majority party)
• Can seek information from the Prime Minister (Art. 78)
2\. Legislative Powers
• Integral part of Parliament (Art. 79)
• Summons, prorogues and dissolves Lok Sabha
• Addresses Parliament (Art. 87)
• Assents to Bills (Art. 111) – Absolute Veto, Suspensive Veto, Pocket Veto
• Promulgates Ordinances when Parliament is not in session (Art. 123)
• Nominates 12 members to Rajya Sabha
3\. Judicial Powers
• Appoints Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts
• Power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, suspend or commute sentences (Art. 72)
• Can seek advisory opinion of Supreme Court (Art. 143) – not binding
4\. Emergency Powers
• National Emergency (Art. 352)
• President’s Rule / State Emergency (Art. 356)
• Financial Emergency (Art. 360)
5\. Military & Diplomatic Powers
• Supreme Commander of Armed Forces
• Declares war and concludes peace (on advice of CoM)
• Appoints Ambassadors and High Commissioners
Important Discretionary Powers (Limited)
• Appointment of Prime Minister in case of hung Parliament
• Dismissal of government that has lost majority
• Dissolution of Lok Sabha
• Pocket Veto
• Returning advice of Council of Ministers for reconsideration (once – 44th Amendment)

• President is Head of the State, not Head of the Government.
• Not directly elected.
• Nominated members do not vote in Presidential election.
• Can return a Bill only once (except Money Bill).
• Ordinance-making power is co-extensive with legislative power of Parliament.

Vice-President
Constitutional Position
• Article 63: There shall be a Vice-President of India.
• Second-highest constitutional office (next to the President in the Order of Precedence).
• Modelled on the American Vice-President.
• Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Art. 64).
Election (Art. 66)
• Indirect election by an Electoral College consisting of:
o Members of both Houses of Parliament (elected + nominated).
• State Legislative Assemblies do NOT participate (major difference from Presidential election).
• Method: Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote + Secret Ballot.
• All doubts and disputes regarding election decided by the Supreme Court (Art. 71) – decision is final.
Qualifications (Art. 66(3))
1\. Citizen of India 2. Completed 35 years of age 3. Qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha 4. Does not hold any office of profit
Term, Resignation & Removal
• Term: 5 years (Art. 67)
• Eligible for re-election any number of times.
• Resignation addressed to the President.
• Can be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Art. 67(b)).
o No formal impeachment like the President. o 14 days’ notice required.
Functions
1\. Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha
o Presides over the sittings of Rajya Sabha.
o Has a casting vote in case of a tie. o Does not preside when a resolution for his removal is under consideration. 2. Acts as President (Art. 65)
o When the office of President falls vacant due to death, resignation, removal or
otherwise. o When the President is unable to discharge his functions (absence, illness, etc.). o Maximum period as Acting President: 6 months (election for new President must
be held within 6 months).
Salary & Emoluments

• When acting as President → en tled to salary, allowances and privileges of the President.
Important Differences: President vs Vice-President
Feature President Vice-President Electoral College MPs + MLAs of States &
UTs Only Members of Parliament Qualification for House Lok Sabha Rajya Sabha Removal Impeachment (both
Houses)
Resolution by Rajya Sabha + agreement of Lok Sabha Resignation to addressed
Vice-President President
Part of Parliament Yes (integral part) No

• Longest-serving → Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (two terms)
• Only person to serve two full terms as Vice-President → Mohammad Hamid Ansari
• Oath administered by → President
• Does not take part in the election of the President as a nominated member? (Nominated MPs do vote in Vice-Presidential election)

o State MLAs do not vote in Vice-Presidential election. o Vice-President is not a member of either House of Parliament. o Not appointed by the President (he is elected). o Salary as Vice-President is not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

Collective Responsibility (Art. 164(2))

Governor
Constitutional Position
• Nominal / Constitutional Head of the State (Real executive is the Chief Minister + Council of Ministers).

• Article 154: Executive power of the State is vested in the Governor.

• Holds office during the pleasure of the President (Art. 156).
• Normal term: 5 years (can be removed earlier or continue longer).
Qualifications (Art. 157 & 158)
1\. Citizen of India 2. Completed 35 years of age 3. Should not be a member of Parliament or State Legislature (if he is, he must vacate the
seat) 4. Should not hold any office of profit
Appointment, Oath & Salary

• Oath administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court (Art. 159).
• Emoluments and allowances charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 202).

Powers of the Governor
1\. Executive Powers
• Appoints the Chief Minister and other Ministers (on advice of CM).
• Appoints Advocate-General, State Election Commissioner, Chairman & members of SPSC, etc.
• Can seek information from the Chief Minister (Art. 167).
• Can recommend President’s Rule under Article 356.
2\. Legislative Powers
• Integral part of the State Legislature (Art. 168).
• Summons, prorogues and dissolves the Legislative Assembly.
• Addresses the State Legislature (Art. 176).
• Assents to Bills, withholds assent, or reserves the Bill for the consideration of the President (Art. 200).
• Promulgates Ordinances when the Legislature is not in session (Art. 213).
• Nominates members to the Legislative Council (if the State has one) – 1/6th of total strength.
3\. Judicial Powers
• Power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, suspend or commute sentences (Art. 161) – only for offences against State laws.

4\. Discretionary Powers
• Appointment of Chief Minister in case of hung Assembly.
• Dismissal of Council of Ministers that has lost majority.
• Dissolution of Legislative Assembly.
• Reserving a Bill for the consideration of the President.
• Recommending President’s Rule (Art. 356).
• Special responsibility in certain States (e.g., Sixth Schedule areas, Tribal areas, etc.).
Special Provisions
• Fifth Schedule: Governor has special responsibility for Scheduled Areas. Submits report to the President.
• Sixth Schedule: Special powers regarding Autonomous District Councils.
• Immunity under Article 361: No criminal proceedings during term of office; civil proceedings only after 2 months’ notice.
Key Differences: Governor vs President

Classification & Types of Bills
1\. Ordinary Bill (Art. 107, 108)
• Introduced in either House (Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha)
• Passed by simple majority; joint sitting (Art. 108) possible in case of deadlock
• Rajya Sabha has no fixed constitutional time limit to consider it
2\. Money Bill (Art. 109, 110)
• Introduced only in Lok Sabha with prior recommendation of President
• Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days (cannot amend or reject)
• Lok Sabha Speaker’s decision under Art. 110(3) is final; No Joint Sitting
• Includes taxes, borrowings, custody of/withdrawal from Consolidated Fund; does not include mere fines/penalties
3\. Financial Bill (I) — Art. 117(1)
• Contains matters of Art. 110 + general legislation
• Introduced only in Lok Sabha on President's recommendation
• Rajya Sabha has full power to reject/amend; Joint Sitting is possible
4\. Financial Bill (II) — Art. 117(3)
• Involves expenditure from Consolidated Fund of India without Art. 110 matters
• Introduced in either House; President's recommendation needed before consideration; Joint Sitting is possible
5\. Constitution Amendment Bill (Art. 368)
• Introduced in either House (no prior recommendation needed; cannot originate in State Legislature)
• Passed by each House separately by Special Majority (majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting)
• Certain federal provisions require ratification by ≥ 1/2 State Legislatures
• No Joint Sitting; President shall give assent (no veto)

Return once

• Joint Sitting (Art. 108): Summoned by President (expresses intention); presided over by Lok Sabha Speaker (if absent → Deputy Speaker → Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha). Quorum is 1/10th; decides by simple majority.
• Effect of Dissolution of Lok Sabha:

o Bill pending in Lok Sabha → Lapses o Bill passed by Lok Sabha but pending in Rajya Sabha → Lapses o Bill pending in Rajya Sabha but not passed by Lok Sabha → Does NOT lapse o Bill with Joint Sitting notified by President → Does NOT lapse o Prorogation does not cause any Bill to lapse.
• State Legislature Bills:
o Legislative Council delaying power for Ordinary Bill = 3 months (1st time) + 1
month (2nd time) = 4 months max. o State Money Bill (Art. 198, 199, 207) → Originates in Legislative Assembly on
Governor’s recommendation; Council gets 14 days. o Governor can reserve a State Bill for President under Art. 200; President
considers under Art. 201.

The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act became effective in 2006.
The Maintenance of Internal Security Act was enacted in 1971.

The Maintenance of Internal Security Act was not a social welfare act.
Acts
Company Rule: Key Acts (1773–1853)
• Regulating Act, 1773: Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings); Supreme Court established at Calcutta (1774, Chief Justice Elijah Impey); banned private trade/bribes.
• Pitt’s India Act, 1784: Established Dual Control Board of Control (Political affairs) + Court of Directors (Commercial affairs).
• Act of 1786: Governor-General empowered to override his Council and assume powers of Commander-in-Chief (first enjoyed by Lord Cornwallis).
• Charter Act, 1813: Abolished Company trade monopoly in India except for Tea and China trade; permitted Christian missionaries; allocated ₹1 lakh annual grant for Indian education.

• Charter Act, 1833: Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck); Company lost commercial status entirely; added 4th member as Law Member (Macaulay); Section 87 barred discrimination in Company service.
• Charter Act, 1853: First clear separation of Legislative and Executive functions of Governor-General’s Council; introduced Open Competition for Civil Services.
Crown Rule & Council Reforms (1858–1947)

• Government of India Act, 1858: Transferred rule from Company to British Crown; Governor-General designated as Viceroy (Lord Canning); abolished Board of Control/Court of Directors; created Secretary of State for India (assisted by 15-member Council).

• Indian Councils Act, 1861: Restored legislative powers of Bombay and Madras (decentralization); initiated Indian participation in law-making; introduced Portfolio System and Viceroy's Ordinance Power (max 6 months).

• Indian Councils Act, 1892: Permitted discussion on Budget and addressing questions to executive (6 days prior notice); supplementary questions and budget voting were not allowed; introduced indirect election principle.

• Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms): Introduced Separate Electorates for Muslims; allowed supplementary questions; first Indian appointed to Viceroy’s Executive Council (Satyendra Prasad Sinha).

• Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms): Introduced Dyarchy in Provinces; introduced Direct Elections and Bicameralism at Centre; separated Central and Provincial budgets; established the Chamber of Princes.
• Government of India Act, 1935: Introduced Provincial Autonomy (abolished provincial dyarchy); proposed (unimplemented) All-India Federation and Central Dyarchy;
established Federal Court (1937, CJ Maurice Gwyer); basis for President’s Ordinance Power (Art. 123).
• Indian Independence Act, 1947: Ended British sovereignty; created two independent Dominions (India and Pakistan); Constituent Assemblies given dual constitution-making and legislative powers.
Key Differences: Landmark Constitutional Reform Acts

Key Constitutional Amendment Acts
• 42nd Amendment (1976): "Mini-Constitution"; inserted Fundamental Duties (Part IVA / Art. 51A); added Socialist, Secular, Integrity to Preamble.
• 44th Amendment (1978): Nullified emergency-era distortions; restored fundamental safeguards.
• 52nd Amendment (1985): Enacted Anti-Defection Law; inserted the 10th Schedule (amended Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191).
• 73rd & 74th Amendments (1992): Constitutional status to Panchayati Raj (Part IX, Arts. 243–243O, 3-tier system) and Municipalities (Part IXA, Arts. 243P–243ZG).
• 84th Amendment (2001): Froze Lok Sabha seat allocations based on the 1971 Census up to the year 2026.
• 86th Amendment (2002): Inserted the 11th Fundamental Duty under Art. 51A(k) regarding education of children.
• 91st Amendment (2003): Strengthened anti-defection provisions and limited council of ministers' size.
• 99th Amendment (2014): Created National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC); declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in 2015.
Major Governance & Statutory Acts
• Representation of the People Act, 1950: Framework for seat allocation, electoral rolls, and Legislative Council composition (Sec. 10 / Sched. 3 / Art. 171).

• Representation of the People Act, 1951: Registration of political parties by ECI; conduct of elections; disqualification upon conviction (≥ 2 years imprisonment disqualified during term + 6 years post-release).
• Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993: Enforced on 28 Sept 1993; established NHRC, SHRCs, and Human Rights Courts for life, liberty, equality, and dignity.
• Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005: Assented 15 June 2005, effective 12 October 2005; legal right supporting transparency/accountability (Namit Sharma Case, 2012; rooted in MKSS movement).

• Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013: 5-member Selection Committee (PM as Chair, LS Speaker, LS LoP, CJI/SC nominee, Eminent Jurist; Rajya Sabha Chairman is NOT a member); min age 45 years; covers PM and public servants inside/outside India.
Imp Facts
• 1861 vs 1935 (Ordinance): Viceroy's Ordinance power originates in the Indian Councils Act, 1861, whereas Art. 123 of the Indian Constitution is modeled after Section 42 of the GoI Act, 1935.
• 1813 vs 1833 (Monopoly): Trade monopoly in India was partially abolished in 1813 (retained Tea + China) and completely abolished in 1833.
• 1919 vs 1935 (Dyarchy): Provincial Dyarchy = 1919; Central Dyarchy proposed = 1935.
• High Courts Act, 1861: High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras established in 1862.
• Social/Security Acts: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (23 sections, effective 1990); PWDVA, 2005 (effective 2006); MISA, 1971 was an internal security statute, not a social welfare act.

Constitutional Amendments
• Article 368 (Part XX) governs the amendment powers and procedure of the Indian Constitution, balancing flexibility and rigidity.
• 3 Methods of Amendment:
o Simple Majority (Outside Art. 368): Creation/alteration of States (Art. 3),
creation/abolition of State Legislative Councils (Art. 169), salaries of judges/officials. o Special Majority (Under Art. 368): Passed by each House separately by a
majority of the total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting. o Special Majority + Ratification by ≥ 1/2 State Legislatures: Required for federal
provisions (e.g., Presidential election, Union/State executive & legislative relations, Supreme Court & High Courts, 7th Schedule Lists, Art. 368 itself, GST Council).
Crucial Rules
• Initiation: Constitution Amendment Bill can originate in either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (cannot be introduced in State Legislatures).
• Prior Recommendation: Prior recommendation of the President is NOT required.
• No Joint Sitting: Each House must pass the Bill independently with special majority; if one House rejects it, the Bill fails completely.
• Presidential Assent: President must give assent (no veto/return power; made mandatory via 24th Amendment, 1971).

• Federal Ratification List: Requires ratification by simple majority of ≥ 1/2 States (not all States). First amendment requiring State ratification was the 3rd Amendment, 1954 (Entry 33, Concurrent List).
o Trap: Qualifications, conditions of office, and tenure of the President do NOT
require State ratification.
Imp Amendments
Amendment Year Core Provisions & Significance
1st 1951 Added 9th Schedule, Arts. 31A, 31B, 15(4); protected agrarian/land
reforms from judicial review.
24th 1971 Affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights; made
President’s assent compulsory.

"Mini Constitution"; added Socialist, Secular, Integrity to Preamble; added Part IVA (Art. 51A) with 10 Fundamental Duties; added DPSPs 39A, 43A; shifted Education to Concurrent List; added Part XIV-A.

(NCT) of Delhi (Art. 239AA).

243ZG) & 12th Schedule (18 subjects).

seats based on 1971 Census up to 2026.

89th 2003 Bifurcated National Commission for SCs/STs into NCSC (Art. 338)
and NCST (Art. 338A).

Added right to form Co-operative Societies (Art. 19(1)(c)), DPSP Art. 43B, and Part IX-B (Arts. 243ZH–243ZT; max 21 directors under Art. 243ZJ).
99th 2014 Created NJAC; struck down as unconstitutional by Supreme Court in 2015 for violating judicial independence.

(exchange of 111 Indian and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves).

created GST Council (Art. 279A).

their own SEBCs (Socially and Educationally Backward Classes).
Schedules & Parts Added by Amendments
• 9th Schedule: Added by 1st Amendment (1951) -- Validation of certain Acts/Regulations (Land reforms).
• 10th Schedule: Added by 52nd Amendment (1985) -- Anti-Defection provisions.
• 11th Schedule: Added by 73rd Amendment (1992) -- 29 Functional items for Panchayats.

• Part IV-A: Added by 42nd Amendment (1976) -- Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A).
• Part IX-A: Added by 74th Amendment (1992) -- Municipalities (Arts. 243P–243ZG).
• Part IX-B: Added by 97th Amendment (2011) -- Co-operative Societies (Arts. 243ZH– 243ZT).

Imp Cases
Amendment Power & Basic Structure Chain

• Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965): Reaffirmed that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
• Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967): Reversed earlier rulings; held that Parliament CANNOT amend Fundamental Rights (first time Parliament's amending power was limited).

• Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): 13-Judge Bench propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine; held Parliament can amend FRs but cannot alter/destroy the Basic Structure; recognized the Preamble as part of the Constitution.
• Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Reinforced the Basic Structure doctrine; struck down clauses giving absolute precedence to DPSPs over FRs; restored the balance between Part III and Part IV.
Key Fundamental Rights & Governance Landmark Cases
• A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950): Narrow interpretation of Article 21; focused on "procedure established by law" concerning preventive detention.
• Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Held that in case of conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs; led directly to the 1st Constitutional Amendment, 1951 (inserted Art. 15(4) for reservations).
• Berubari Union Case (1960): Held that the Preamble is NOT an integral part of the Constitution (later overturned by Kesavananda Bharati and S.R. Bommai).
• Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): Struck down parts of the 39th Amendment that barred judicial review of election disputes of the PM and Speaker.

• Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): Widened Article 21 (Right to Travel Abroad); procedure must be "just, fair, and reasonable"; established the golden triangle (Arts. 14, 19, and 21 are mutually inclusive).
• P. Sambamurthy v. State of A.P. (1987): Challenged and struck down portions of the 32nd Constitutional Amendment.
• Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillu (1993): Upheld the validity of the 52nd Amendment (10th Schedule - Anti-Defection Law); held that Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review.

• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): Laid guidelines against arbitrary misuse of Article 356 (President's Rule); made proclamation subject to judicial review; held secularism and federalism as basic features; reaffirmed Preamble as an integral part.

Election Commission
• Constitutional Status: Permanent, independent, constitutional body under Part XV (Articles 324–329).
• Established on 25 January 1950 (celebrated annually as National Voters' Day since 2011).
• Article 324(1): Vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the Election Commission of India (ECI).
• Mandate covers elections to: Parliament (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), State Legislatures (Assemblies & Councils), President, and Vice-President.
• Local body elections (Panchayats and Municipalities) are NOT conducted by ECI; they fall under the State Election Commission (SEC) under Articles 243K & 243ZA.
Composition, Appointment & Removal

• Composition: 1 Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) + 2 Election Commissioners (multi- member body established continuously since 1 October 1993). All three have equal powers, salary equivalent to Supreme Court Judges, and decide by majority.
• Appointment: By the President of India.
• Tenure: 6 years or up to 65 years of age, whichever is earlier.
• Removal Safeguards:
o CEC: Removed only in like manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court
Judge (Art. 324(5)). o Other ECs & Regional Commissioners: Removed by the President on the
recommendation of the CEC.
Key Differences: ECI vs State Election Commission (SEC)
Feature Election Commission of India
(ECI) State Election Commission (SEC)

Core Functions, Disqualifications & Powers
• Electoral Rolls & Suffrage:
o Art. 325: Single general electoral roll; no discrimination based on religion, race,
caste, or sex. o Art. 326: Universal Adult Suffrage for Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies. o Voting Age: Reduced from 21 to 18 years via the 61st Amendment Act, 1988
(effective 1989). o Nature of Right to Vote: A Legal/Statutory Right (Kuldip Nayar Case), not a
Fundamental Right.
• Disqualification Role:
o MPs (Art. 103): Decided by the President based on the binding opinion of the
ECI. o MLAs/MLCs (Art. 192): Decided by the Governor based on the binding opinion
of the ECI.

• Party Registration & Symbols: Registers political parties under RPA 1951; allots symbols and decides recognition under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968; adjudicates party merger/split disputes.
• Model Code of Conduct (MCC): Formulated and enforced by ECI from the date of election schedule announcement (ECI-formulated guideline, NOT an Act of Parliament).
National Party Criteria (Any One Condition)
• ≥2% of Lok Sabha seats won from at least 3 different States, OR
• ≥6% of valid votes polled in Lok Sabha/Assembly elections in ≥4 States + at least 4 Lok Sabha seats, OR
• Recognized as a State Party in at least 4 States.
Imp Facts
• Notification: Election notifications are issued by the President (Parliament) or Governor (State Legislature)—NOT by the ECI. ECI only recommends dates and determines the schedule.

• Delimitation Commission vs ECI: Constituency delimitation is executed by an independent Delimitation Commission set up under parliamentary law, whose orders cannot be questioned in court or modified by legislatures.
• Candidature Limits (RPA 1951, Sec. 33): A candidate can contest from a maximum of 2 constituencies (Lok Sabha or State Assembly).
• Forfeiture of Security Deposit: Occurs if a candidate fails to secure more than 1/6th of total valid votes polled.
• Election Reforms Chronology: EVM (1982, Parur, Kerala) → EPIC Voter ID (1993) → VVPAT (Sept 2013, Noksen, Nagaland) → NOTA (Sept 2013).
• Key Personalities: Sukumar Sen (1st CEC, 1950–58); V. S. Ramadevi (1st Woman CEC, 1990).
• Simultaneous Elections (ONOE) Articles: Potentially requires amending Arts. 83, 85, 172, 174, and 356.

Finance Commission
• Constitutional Status: Permanent, independent, quasi-judicial constitutional body under Article 280 (Part XII).
• Constituted by the President of India every 5 years or earlier as deemed necessary (not strictly/rigidly every 5 years).
• First Commission: Constituted under Presidential order in 1951, set up on 6 April 1952 under Chairman K.C. Neogy.
• Core Function: Anchor of Fiscal Federalism; recommends the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Union and States, and the allocation among States.
Composition & Qualifications
• Composition (Art. 280(1)): Total 5 members → 1 Chairman + 4 other members appointed by the President.
• Qualifications (Art. 280(2)): Determined by Parliament by law (NOT determined by the President or Union Cabinet).

Core Functions (Art. 280(3)) & Report Submission (Art. 281)

• Submission of Report (Art. 281): Submits its report to the President, who causes it to be laid before both Houses of Parliament along with an explanatory memorandum on action taken ( Trap: Report is laid by the President, NOT the Finance Minister).

Lok Sabha: Rules of Procedure & Conduct of Business
• The Constitution provides the broad institutional framework; day-to-day proceedings in Lok Sabha are governed by the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.
• Crucial Exam Distinction: Several major parliamentary tools (e.g., No-Confidence Motion, Zero Hour, Rule 377) are NOT mentioned in the Constitution—they derive from Rules or procedural conventions.
• Primary mechanisms for executive accountability: Question Hour, Supplementary Questions, and Adjournment Motions.
Motions & Important Rules
• No-Confidence Motion (Rule 198):
o Not mentioned in the Constitution; introduced ONLY in Lok Sabha. o Moved against the entire Council of Ministers (cannot be moved against an
individual minister). o Requires written notice to the Secretary-General and the support of at least 50
members for leave to be granted.
• Confidence Motion: Moved by the Council of Ministers/Government to demonstrate majority support on the floor.
• Rule 184 (Discussion + Voting): Permits discussion on a specific matter of public interest followed by voting (carries significant political consequences for the government).

• Rule 377 (Special Mention of Matters): Allows members to raise matters of general public importance that cannot be raised under rules governing Questions, Calling Attention, or other formal Motions; requires written notice and Speaker's consent (increased from 20 to 30 matters/day in 2015).
• Rule 8(1): Governs the procedure for the election of the Deputy Speaker (date fixed by the Speaker and notified by the Secretary-General).

Types of Parliamentary Questions
• Starred Question: Requires an oral answer on the floor; supplementary questions are ALLOWED (max 20 starred questions listed for oral answer per day).
• Unstarred Question: Requires a written answer laid on the table; supplementary questions are NOT allowed.
• Short Notice Question: Pertains to an urgent matter of public importance; asked with notice shorter than 10 clear days; receives an oral answer; supplementary questions are ALLOWED.
Debate Regulation & Other Motions
• Adjournment Motion:
o Interrupts normal business to discuss a definite matter of urgent public
importance and recent occurrence. o Involves an element of censure/condemnation against the government.
• Calling Attention Motion:
o Indian parliamentary innovation to draw the attention of a Minister to an
urgent matter of public importance.
o Resembles an Adjournment Motion but does NOT contain an element of
censure/condemnation.
• Closure Motion & Guillotine:

o Closure Motion: Moved to cut short debate and put the question to vote. o Guillotine: A form of closure applied when allotted time expires all remaining discussed and undiscussed clauses/demands are immediately put to vote.
Important Facts:
• Article vs Rule Matching:
o No-Confidence Motion: Lok Sabha Rule 198 (NOT an Article). o Rule 184: Substantive motion requiring discussion with voting. o Money Bill / Joint Sitting: Constitutional (Arts. 110 & 108).
• Negative Traps:

o Zero Hour is NOT a constitutional provision. o No-Confidence Motion can NOT be moved in Rajya Sabha. o Unstarred questions do NOT allow supplementary questions. o Calling Attention does NOT carry censure/condemnation against the
government.

Chief Justice & Supreme Court
• Constitutional Status: Head of the Union Judiciary and the Supreme Court of India under Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147).
• Appointment: Appointed by the President of India under Article 124(2); by convention, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court is appointed as Chief Justice of India (CJI).
• Tenure & Retirement: Holds office until attaining the age of 65 years (no fixed term in years).
• Oath: Administered by the President (or a person appointed by the President) under the Third Schedule.
• Resignation: Addressed in writing to the President of India.

Appointment, Collegium & Removal Procedures
• Collegium Evolution:
o First Judges Case (1981): "Consultation" does not mean "concurrence";
executive supremacy in judicial appointments. o Second Judges Case (1993): "Consultation" means "concurrence"; introduced
the Collegium system (CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges). o Third Judges Case (1998): Expanded the Collegium to CJI + 4 senior-most SC
judges for SC appointments. o 99th Amendment & NJAC (2014–15): National Judicial Appointments
Commission struck down as unconstitutional to preserve the Independence of the Judiciary (Basic Structure).
• Removal Procedure (Art. 124(4)):
o Removed by an order of the President after an address by Parliament. o Grounds: Proved misbehaviour or incapacity. o Majority Required: Special Majority in each House (majority of total
membership + ≥ 2/3 of members present and voting in the same session). o Governed procedurally by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
Key Jurisdictional Powers of the Supreme Court
• Original Jurisdiction (Art. 131): Exclusive jurisdiction over federal disputes (Centre ↔ State or State ↔ State). Does not cover pre-Constitution treaties or inter-State water disputes (Art. 262).
• Writ Jurisdiction (Art. 32): Fundamental Right to approach the SC directly for enforcement of Part III rights (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo- Warranto).
• Advisory Jurisdiction (Art. 143):

o On question of law/public importance: SC may tender or refuse advice. o On pre-Constitution disputes: SC is bound to give advice. o In all cases, the advice tendered is not binding on the President.
Procedural Distinctions
• Acting CJI vs Ad Hoc Judge:
o Acting CJI (Art. 126): Appointed by the President when the CJI is unable to
perform duties. o Ad Hoc Judge (Art. 127): Appointed by the CJI (with previous consent of the
President and consultation with the concerned HC Chief Justice) to meet a lack of quorum.
• Removal vs Appointment: The President appoints SC judges in consultation/collegium concurrence, but removal requires a statutory inquiry + parliamentary special majority address under Art. 124(4).
• Court of Record (Art. 129): Judgments have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any subordinate court; includes power to punish for contempt.

Feature Question Hour Zero Hour Procedure in Rules Maximum Duration 1 Hour Generally up to 1 Hour (Lok Sabha) Core Purpose Questioning Ministers on administrative actions Raising urgent matters of public importance without prior notice Calling Attention vs Adjournment Motion Feature Calling Attention Motion Adjournment Motion Origin Indian parliamentary innovation Traditional parliamentary device Primary Objective Call attention of a Minister to an urgent public matter Discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance Impact on Business Does not disrupt the scheduled daily agenda Interrupts and suspends normal parliamentary business Element of Censure NO condemnation / censure element Involves censure/condemnation of the Government Procedural Effect Restricted the scope of Adjournment Motion Admissible only when other tools (e.g., Short Duration) are too late

Local Self-Government  Core Principle: Exercise in democratic decentralisation, community participation, and local accountability (NOT central control or mere administration).  Constitutional Directive: Article 40 (DPSP) directs the State to organize Village Panchayats as units of self-government.  Historical Landmarks: o Charles Metcalfe: Described Indian village communities as "Little Republics". o Lord Ripon (1882 Resolution): Recognized as the Father of Local Self- Government in India. o GoI Act, 1919: Local Self-Government made a Transferred Subject under provincial dyarchy. o First Panchayati Raj State: Rajasthan (Nagaur District on 2 October 1959), followed second by Andhra Pradesh. o First Municipal Corporation: Madras (1688). Evolution: Landmark Committees  Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957): Recommended 3-tier Panchayati Raj (Gram Panchayat  -- Panchayat Samiti  -- Zila Parishad); recognized as the Architect of Panchayati Raj.  Ashok Mehta Committee (1977–78): Recommended a 2-tier model and separate Nyaya Panchayats.  Hanumantha Rao Committee (1983): Decentralisation of powers/finance and district planning bodies.  G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985): Revitalization and representative character of Panchayats.  L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986): Recommended constitutional status and greater financial resources for local bodies.

Direct Comparison: 73rd vs 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts (1992) Feature 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 74th Amendment Act, 1992 Domain Rural Local Self-Government (Panchayats) Urban Local Self-Government (Municipalities) Enforcement Date 24 April 1993 (National Panchayati Raj Day) 1 June 1993 Constitutional Part Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) Part IX-A (Articles 243P to 243ZG) Schedule & Items 11th Schedule (29 Functional Subjects) 12th Schedule (18 Functional Subjects) Institutional Tiers • Village: Gram Panchayat
• Block: Panchayat Samiti
• District: Zila Parishad • Transitional Area: Nagar Panchayat
• Smaller Urban: Municipal Council
• Larger Urban: Municipal Corporation Key Planning Bodies Interlinked with District Planning DPC (Art. 243ZD) & MPC (Art. 243ZE)

Imp Articles  Art. 243A (Gram Sabha): Village-level general assembly of all persons registered in the village electoral rolls.  Art. 243B (Three-Tier System & Exemption): Mandatory 3-tier structure; Intermediate tier (Panchayat Samiti) is optional for States with a population ≤20 Lakhs.  Art. 243C & 243R (Composition & Age): State Legislature regulates composition; minimum qualifying age is 21 years (for both Panchayats and Municipalities).  Art. 243D & 243T (Reservations): Mandatory reservation of not less than 1/3rd (≥33%) of total seats and chairpersons for women.  Art. 243E & 243U (Tenure & Dissolution): Fixed term of 5 years; if dissolved prematurely, elections must be held within 6 months (not required if remaining term is < 6 months).  Art. 243G & 243W (Powers & Responsibilities): Powers over economic development, social justice, sanitation, public health, local utilities, and roads/bridges.  Art. 243-I & 243-Y (State Finance Commission): Constituted every 5 years by the Governor to review local finance distribution.  Art. 243J & 243Z (Accounts & Audit): State Legislature provides for maintenance and audit of accounts.  Art. 243K & 243ZA (State Election Commission): Superintendence, direction, and conduct of local elections. Traps:  Functional Domain Trap: Local Self-Government includes public health, sanitation, water supply, and rural development; Maintenance of Public Order and Judicial Review are NOT local-government functions.  Gram Sabha vs Gram Panchayat: Gram Sabha is the entire electorate (body of registered voters); Gram Panchayat is the elected executive body.  Audit Authority Trap: Panchayat audit laws are enacted by the State Legislature (NOT the Union Parliament, CAG, or District Collector).  Intermediate Level Exemption: Populated threshold where intermediate tier is optional is 20 Lakhs.

Prorogation terminates a session and may be effected by the President or Governor.

Terminology Parliamentary Sittings, Sessions & Procedures  Summoning: The President calls each House of Parliament to meet under Article 85; the maximum gap between two sessions cannot exceed 6 months.  Session: The period between the first sitting of a House and its prorogation or dissolution (Standard sessions: Budget, Monsoon, Winter).  Sitting: A daily meeting of the House during a session (comprises morning and post- lunch sittings).  Adjournment: Terminates a daily sitting for a specified time (hours, days, or weeks); exercised by the Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman).  Adjournment Sine Die: Terminating a sitting without assigning a day for reassembly.  Prorogation: Terminates a session of the House (not the House itself); issued by the President under Article 85(2).  Dissolution: Ends the life of the House entirely; applies only to Lok Sabha (Rajya Sabha is a permanent House).  Recess: The period between the prorogation of a session and the commencement of a new session (e.g., when Parliament is in recess, the President may issue ordinances under Art. 123).  Quorum: The minimum number of members required to be present to conduct official business (1/10th of total membership of the House under Art. 100).  Question Hour: The first hour of every sitting dedicated to asking and answering questions.  Zero Hour: An Indian parliamentary innovation (since early 1960s) following Question Hour to raise urgent public matters without prior formal notice.  Closure Motion: A motion moved to cut short debate and put the matter directly to vote.  Guillotine: A specific form of closure where, upon the expiry of allotted time, all undiscussed clauses or demands for grants are put to vote immediately.

Direct Comparison: Key Motions & Questions Motion / Device Primary Target / Purpose Procedural Rule / Key Distinction No-Confidence Motion Tests majority support of Council of Ministers Moved only in Lok Sabha; governed by Rule 198; needs 50 members' support; no reasons required. Confidence Motion Proves majority support on the floor Moved by the Council of Ministers/Government. Censure Motion Expresses strong disapproval/criticism of specific policies Moved against an individual minister or entire council; specific reasons must be stated. Calling Attention Draws a Minister's attention to an urgent public matter Indian innovation; does NOT contain an element of censure/condemnation. Adjournment Motion Suspends business for an urgent matter of public importance Carries an element of censure/condemnation; interrupts normal business. Starred Question Requires an Oral Answer Supplementary questions ALLOWED; limit: 20 oral questions/day. Unstarred Question Requires a Written Answer Supplementary questions NOT allowed. Short Notice Question Urgent public matter with shorter notice period Receives an oral answer; supplementary questions ALLOWED.

Financial Terms & Cut Motions  Annual Financial Statement: Constitutional nomenclature for the Union Budget under Article 112.  Appropriation Bill (Art. 114): Statutory authorization enabling withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of India for voted grants and charged expenditure.  Vote on Account (Art. 116): Advance grant given by Lok Sabha to cover estimated expenditure for a part of the financial year pending budget passage.  Vote of Credit: An unexpected, blank-check financial grant for an emergency or indefinite demand whose details cannot be stated in a budget.  Charged Expenditure: Non-votable expenditure paid directly out of the Consolidated Fund of India (can only be discussed).  The Three Cut Motions: o Policy Cut: Move to reduce the demand to ₹1 (expresses complete disapproval of the underlying policy). o Economy Cut: Move to reduce the demand by a specified amount (demands economy in expenditure). o Token Cut: Move to reduce the demand by ₹100 (ventilates a specific grievance within the Government's sphere of responsibility). Constitutional Writs & Judicial Concepts  Habeas Corpus ("To have the body"): Quashes illegal or unlawful physical detention.  Mandamus ("We Command"): Directs a public official, inferior court, or statutory authority to perform a mandatory public/legal duty.  Prohibition ("To Forbid"): Issued by a higher court to prevent an inferior court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction (preventive).  Certiorari ("To be Certified"): Issued by a higher court to quash an order already passed by an inferior court/tribunal due to lack of jurisdiction or error of law (curative and preventive).  Quo-Warranto ("By what warrant/authority"): Inquires into the legality of a person's claim to a public office to prevent illegal usurpation.  Judicial Review: Inherent power of constitutional courts to review legislative enactments and executive actions against constitutional validity.  Basic Structure Doctrine: Propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973); core structural features of the Constitution that cannot be abrogated or destroyed even via Article 368. Executive Pardoning Powers (Art. 72 & Art. 161)  Pardon: Completely absorbs and removes both the sentence and conviction, placing the offender in the same position as if the offense had never been committed.  Commutation: Substitutes a heavier form of punishment with a lighter form (e.g., Death sentence -- Rigorous Life Imprisonment).

 Remission: Reduces the period/duration of the sentence without changing its fundamental character (e.g., 2 years rigorous imprisonment  -- 1 year rigorous imprisonment).  Respite: Awards a lesser sentence in place of the original penalty due to special personal circumstances (e.g., pregnancy, mental/physical disability).  Reprieve: Grants a temporary stay or postponement of the execution of a sentence (especially death penalty) to allow time to seek Presidential pardon. Electoral Systems & Federal Governance Terms  First-Past-the-Post (FPTP): Plurality voting system where the candidate securing the highest number of valid votes is declared elected (absolute majority >50% not required).  Proportional Representation by Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV): Multi-preference quota-based indirect voting system used for President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha, and Legislative Councils to ensure proportional representation.  Delimitation: The statutory process of redrawing territorial constituency boundaries based on recent census figures to enforce equal representation.  Dyarchy ("Double Rule"): System introduced in provinces under the GoI Act, 1919, splitting administrative subjects into Reserved (Governor + Executive Council) and Transferred (Governor + Popular Ministers).  Collective Responsibility (Art. 75(3)): Principle that the Council of Ministers is collectively answerable to the popular House (Lok Sabha); all ministers sink or swim together. Traps  Adjournment vs Prorogation vs Dissolution: o Adjournment terminates a Sitting (Speaker/Presiding Officer). o Prorogation terminates a Session (President/Governor). o Dissolution terminates the House (President/Governor).  Cut Motion Amounts: Policy Cut = ₹1 | Token Cut = ₹100 | Economy Cut = Specified amount.  Right to Vote: It is a Legal/Statutory Right, not a Fundamental Right.  Local Self-Government Exemption: 3-tier Panchayati Raj applies everywhere, but the Intermediate tier (Panchayat Samiti) is optional in States with a population of ≤20 Lakhs.

State Legislative Assembly  Constitutional Status: Governed under Part VI (Articles 168–212); Article 168 provides that the State Legislature consists of the Governor + Legislative Assembly (+ Legislative Council in bicameral States).  Nature: The Lower, popular House directly elected by citizens on the basis of Universal Adult Suffrage (Art. 326) via the First-Past-the-Post (FPTP) system.  Electoral Authority: Elections to the State Legislative Assembly are conducted by the Election Commission of India (Art. 324), NOT the State Election Commission.  Collective Responsibility (Art. 164(2)): The State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible specifically to the Legislative Assembly. Composition, Numbers & Qualifications (Art. 170 & 173)  Strength Limits (Art. 170): Maximum = 500 members; Minimum standard floor = 60 members.  State Extremes: o Largest Assembly: Uttar Pradesh (403 members). o Smallest State Assembly: Sikkim (32 members) (Special constitutional exception). o Smallest UT Assembly: Puducherry (33 members).  Age Qualification (Art. 173): Minimum 25 years for Legislative Assembly (vs. 30 years for Legislative Council).  Reservations: o Art. 332: Mandatory reservation of seats for SCs and STs based on population ratios. o 104th CAA (2020): Ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Art. 333. o 106th CAA (2023): Provides approx 1/3rd reservation for women in directly elected Assembly seats (effective after post-census delimitation).

Direct Comparison: Legislative Assembly vs Legislative Council Feature Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) House Status Lower / Popular House Upper House / House of Elders Election Mode Direct Election (FPTP) Indirect Election (PR-STV) + Nomination Minimum Age 25 Years 30 Years Prescribed Strength Min: 60 Max: 500 Tenure & Dissolution 5 Years; Subject to Dissolution Permanent body; 1/3rd retire every 2 yrs (6-yr term) Abolition / Creation Cannot be abolished Can be created/abolished under Art. 169 Money Bill Power Sole House of introduction; Final authority Can only delay for 14 days; cannot amend/reject Ordinary Bill Delay Originating / Overriding Chamber Max total delay: 4 months (3 + 1 months) Presiding Officer Speaker (Art. 178) Chairman (Art. 182) Defection Decider Speaker (10th Schedule) Chairman (10th Schedule)

Presiding Officers  Speaker & Deputy Speaker (Art. 178): Elected by the Assembly from among its members.  Resignation (Art. 179): The Speaker submits resignation to the Deputy Speaker; Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker.  Continuation After Dissolution (Universal Trap): When the Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker does NOT vacate office immediately; continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly.  Voting: Speaker cannot vote in the first instance, but exercises a casting vote in case of an equality of votes (tie).  Disqualification Deciding Authority (Art. 192 vs 10th Schedule): o Ordinary Disqualifications (Art. 191/192): Decided by the Governor, who must obtain and act according to the binding opinion of the Election Commission of India. o Defection Disqualifications (10th Schedule): Decided exclusively by the Speaker (subject to judicial review). Legislative Procedure & Governor's Interface  Sessions & Dissolution (Art. 174): The Governor summons, prorogues, and dissolves the Assembly (maximum session gap: 6 months).  Governor's Address (Art. 176): Addressed at the commencement of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year.  Money Bills (Arts. 198 & 199): Introduced only in the Assembly with prior recommendation of the Governor (Art. 207); Speaker's certification is final; Legislative Council has 14 days.  Ordinary Bills (Art. 197): Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill for a maximum of 4 months (3 months first time + 1 month second time); Council cannot permanently block legislation.  Assent & Reservation (Arts. 200 & 201): Governor can give assent, withhold assent, return an ordinary Bill (no fixed time limit), or reserve the Bill for Presidential consideration.  Ordinance Power (Art. 213): Promulgated during legislative recess; ceases to operate 6 weeks after the reassembly of the State Legislature unless approved earlier.  Ministry Size & Non-Member Ministers (Art. 164): o Council of Ministers capped at max 15% of Assembly strength (91st CAA, 2003); minimum 12 ministers (including CM). o A non-member minister can hold office for a maximum of 6 consecutive months without getting elected.

Traps  Article 169 (Council Creation/Abolition): Initiated by Assembly passing a resolution by Special Majority (majority of total membership + ≥2/3 present and voting) enacted into law by Parliament by Simple Majority.  6 Bicameral States: Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.  Term Extension during National Emergency: Parliament can extend the Assembly term for 1 year at a time, up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases.  Articles: o Art. 170: Assembly Composition | Art. 173: Age (25 yrs) | Art. 174: Prorogation/Dissolution o Art. 178 & 179: Speaker election & resignation | Art. 192: Disqualification by Governor o Art. 198 & 199: State Money Bill | Art. 200 & 201: Assent & Reservation | Art. 213: Ordinances

Kihoto Hollohan was linked to the 52nd Constitutional Amendment.
Kihoto Hollohan was linked to the Tenth Schedule.
S.R. Bommai was decided in 1994.
S.R. Bommai held that Article 356 is subject to judicial review.
S.R. Bommai held that secularism is part of the Basic Structure.
S.R. Bommai was linked to Article 356.
S.R. Bommai was linked to Article 355.
Vishaka was decided in 1997.
Vishaka formulated guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace.
Vishaka was linked to Article 14.
Vishaka was linked to Article 19(1)(g).
Vishaka was linked to Article 21.
K.S. Puttaswamy was decided in 2017.
K.S. Puttaswamy was decided by a 9-judge Bench.
K.S. Puttaswamy held that the right to privacy is a Fundamental Right.

K.S. Puttaswamy was linked to Part III.

Shayara Bano declared Talaq-e-Biddat unconstitutional.

Shayara Bano was linked to Article 14.
Shayara Bano was linked to Article 21.

Navtej Singh Johar was linked to Article 15.
Navtej Singh Johar was linked to Article 19.
Navtej Singh Johar was linked to Article 21.
Satwant Singh recognized the right to travel abroad under Article 21 in 1967.

Subhash Kumar recognized the right to a clean environment under Article 21 in 1991.

Olga Tellis recognized the right to shelter under Article 21 in 1985.
Olga Tellis recognized the right to livelihood under Article 21 in 1985.
Chameli Singh recognized the right to shelter under Article 21 in 1995.
Chameli Singh recognized the right to livelihood under Article 21 in 1995.
Lata Singh recognized the right to marry a person of one’s choice under Article 21 in 2006.

Malak Singh further developed the right to privacy under Article 21 in 1980.
Champakam Dorairajan led to the First Constitutional Amendment inserting Article 15(4).
Indra Sawhney upheld the OBC quota.
Indra Sawhney excluded the creamy layer from the OBC quota.

M. Nagaraj was decided in 2006.
M. Nagaraj validated reservation in promotions.
M. Nagaraj made reservation in promotions subject to quantifiable backwardness data.
M. Nagaraj made reservation in promotions subject to efficiency data.

Navtej Singh Johar invalidated provisions of Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code.
Navtej Singh Johar did not invalidate Article 377 of the Constitution.
Bachan Singh held that the death penalty in the “rarest of rare cases” is not unconstitutional under Article 21.
The “rarest of rare” capital-punishment principle is associated with Bachan Singh.
Kesavananda Bharati affirmed that the Preamble is part of the Constitution.
S.R. Bommai affirmed that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
The Supreme Court coined the expression “Caged Parrot” during the Coal Allocation Scam Case in 2013.
The Supreme Court struck down the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act in Sarbananda Sonowal in 2005.
The Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act is also known as the IMDT Act.

Article 355 imposes a duty on the Union to protect States against external aggression.
Article 355 imposes a duty on the Union to protect States against internal disturbance.

Landmark Judgments Comparison: Landmark Constitutional Cases Case Name Year Core Legal Principle / Landmark Ruling Linked Article / Amendment A.K. Gopalan 1950 Narrow interpretation of "Procedure Established by Law"; Preventive Detention Article 21 Champakam Dorairajan 1951 Held FRs prevail over DPSPs in conflict; led to 1st CAA (Art. 15(4)) Articles 15, 29, 37, 46 Shankari Prasad 1951 Parliament CAN amend Fundamental Rights under Art. 368 Article 13 vs Article 368 Berubari Union 1960 Preamble is NOT an integral part of the Constitution Article 3 / Preamble Sajjan Singh 1965 Reaffirmed Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution Article 368 Golaknath 1967 Reversed earlier view; Parliament CANNOT amend Fundamental Rights Article 13(2) vs Article 368 Kesavananda Bharati 1973 13-Judge Bench propounded Basic Structure Doctrine; Preamble is part Article 368 / 24th CAA Indira Nehru Gandhi 1975 Struck down parts of 39th CAA; Free & fair elections in Basic Structure 39th CAA (Art. 329A) Maneka Gandhi 1978 Expanded Art. 21; "Just, fair & reasonable" test; Arts. 14, 19, 21 Golden Triangle Articles 14, 19, 21 Minerva Mills 1980 Reaffirmed Basic Structure; restored balance between Part III & Part IV 42nd CAA (Art. 368 clauses) Indra Sawhney 1992 Upheld 27% OBC reservation; capped total reservations at 50% ceiling Articles 15(4), 16(4)

Case Name Year Core Legal Principle / Landmark Ruling Linked Article / Amendment Kihoto Hollohan 1992/93 Upheld 52nd CAA (10th Schedule); Speaker's defection ruling subject to review 52nd CAA / 10th Schedule S.R. Bommai 1994 Article 356 (President's Rule) subject to Judicial Review; Secularism is Basic Structure Articles 356, 355 Vishaka 1997 Formulated Vishaka Guidelines against workplace sexual harassment Articles 14, 19(1)(g), 21 K.S. Puttaswamy 2017 9-Judge Bench held Right to Privacy is a Fundamental Right Article 21 / Part III Shayara Bano 2017 Declared Talaq-e-Biddat (instant Triple Talaq) unconstitutional & arbitrary Articles 14, 21 Navtej Singh Johar 2018 Decriminalized consensual adult same-sex acts; read down Section 377 IPC Articles 14, 15, 19, 21

 Expanded Rights under Article 21: o Right to Travel Abroad: Satwant Singh (1967) & Maneka Gandhi (1978) o Right to Emergency Medical Aid: Parmanand Katara (1989) o Right to Clean Environment & Air: Subhash Kumar (1991) o Right to Shelter / Livelihood: Olga Tellis (1985) & Chameli Singh (1995) o Right to Marry Person of Choice: Lata Singh (2006) o Right to Privacy: Govind (1975) Malak Singh (1980) K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)  Reservation Jurisprudence: o Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Led to the 1st Constitutional Amendment inserting Art. 15(4). o Indra Sawhney (1992): OBC quota upheld, creamy layer excluded, 50% vertical limit established. o M. Nagaraj (2006): Validated reservation in promotions subject to quantifiable backwardness/efficiency data (Art. 335).  Equal Pay for Equal Work: Delineated in Randhir Singh (1982) by reading Articles 14, 16, and 39(d) with the Preamble.

Traps:  Section 377 IPC vs Article 377: Navtej Singh Johar invalidated provisions of Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, NOT Article 377 of the Constitution.  Capital Punishment (Bachan Singh): Death penalty in the "rarest of rare cases" is NOT unconstitutional under Article 21.  Preamble Status: Berubari (1960) held it is NOT part; Kesavananda (1973) and Bommai (1994) affirmed it IS an integral part of the Constitution.  CBI "Caged Parrot": Coined by the Supreme Court during the Coal Allocation Scam Case (2013).  IMDT Act (Sarbananda Sonowal, 2005): Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act struck down under Article 355 (Duty of Union to protect States against external aggression/internal disturbance).
