x: Prerogative remedies were borrowed from English common law.
The Supreme Court issues writs under Article 32.
High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar designated Article 32 as the “heart and soul of the Constitution.”
Article 32 guarantees a direct and effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies.
The Supreme Court has narrower writ jurisdiction under Article 32.
The Supreme Court issues writs only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights in Part III.
The High Courts have wider writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
The High Courts issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
The High Courts issue writs for any other purpose, including enforcement of ordinary statutory or legal rights.
Parliament may empower any other court by law to exercise all or any powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under Article 32(3).
The other court empowered under Article 32(3) may exercise those powers within its local jurisdiction.
Habeas Corpus literally means “To have the body.”
Habeas Corpus literally means “Let us have the body.”
Habeas Corpus targets public authorities.
Habeas Corpus targets private individuals.
Habeas Corpus releases a person from unlawful or illegal physical detention.
Habeas Corpus safeguards individual liberty.
Habeas Corpus applies whenever detention is illegal.
Habeas Corpus can lie against private persons.
Mandamus literally means “We command.”
Mandamus targets public officials.
Mandamus targets statutory bodies.
Mandamus targets inferior courts.
Mandamus targets tribunals.
Mandamus compels performance of a mandatory public or legal duty.
Mandamus applies when a mandatory public or legal duty has been refused or neglected.
Mandamus does not lie against purely private bodies unless they are discharging a public duty.
Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors.
Prohibition literally means “To forbid.”
Prohibition literally means “To restrain.”
Prohibition targets judicial bodies only.
Prohibition targets quasi-judicial bodies only.
Prohibition prevents an inferior court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction.
Prohibition prevents an inferior court or tribunal from usurping jurisdiction not vested in it.
Prohibition is issued while the proceeding is still pending in the lower body.
Certiorari literally means “To be certified.”
Certiorari literally means “To be informed.”
Certiorari targets judicial bodies.
Certiorari targets quasi-judicial bodies.
Certiorari targets administrative bodies.
Certiorari quashes an illegal order already passed.
Certiorari applies when an order was passed due to lack of jurisdiction.
Certiorari applies when an order was passed due to excess of jurisdiction.
Certiorari applies when an order contains an error of law on the face of the record.
Certiorari is issued after an order or decision is made.
Certiorari provides postmortem review.
Quo-Warranto literally means “By what authority?”
Quo-Warranto literally means “By what warrant?”
Quo-Warranto targets a person holding a substantive public office.
Quo-Warranto targets a person claiming a substantive public office.
Quo-Warranto prevents illegal usurpation of a permanent public office.
The permanent public office addressed by Quo-Warranto must be created by statute or the Constitution.
Any public-minded citizen can move a Quo-Warranto petition.
Quo-Warranto does not require aggrieved-party status.
Prohibition is issued to prevent excess of jurisdiction.
Prohibition operates while a judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding is pending.
Prohibition halts a proceeding involving excess of jurisdiction.
Certiorari is issued to correct or quash an order.
Certiorari operates after an order has been passed.
Certiorari removes or quashes decisions suffering from jurisdictional error.
Habeas Corpus targets illegal custody of a person.
Habeas Corpus provides a remedy for bodily freedom.
Mandamus targets non-performance of a legal duty by a public authority.
Mandamus commands the performance of a lawful public duty.
Quo-Warranto challenges the legal qualification or title of a person holding public office.
Habeas Corpus is the only writ directly applicable against private individuals in cases of illegal confinement.
Mandamus can lie against a government company performing a public function.
Mandamus can lie against a statutory corporation performing a public function.
Any member of the public can file a Quo-Warranto petition.
The traditional locus standi requirement is relaxed in Quo-Warranto proceedings.
A Quo-Warranto petitioner need not be personally aggrieved.

Writs  Constitutional Basis: Prerogative remedies borrowed from English common law; issued by the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226).  Heart and Soul of the Constitution: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar designated Article 32 as the "heart and soul of the Constitution" because it guarantees a direct, effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies.  Scope Comparison (Universal Trap): o Supreme Court (Art. 32): Narrower jurisdiction—issues writs ONLY for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights (Part III). o High Courts (Art. 226): Wider jurisdiction—issues writs for Fundamental Rights AND for any other purpose (enforcement of ordinary statutory/legal rights).  Article 32(3): Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within its local jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court. Comparison: Five Constitutional Writs Writ Name Literal Latin Meaning Primary Target / Body Core Objective / Purpose Procedural Stage Habeas Corpus "To have the body" / "Let us have the body" Public authorities AND Private individuals Release a person from unlawful/illegal physical detention; safeguards individual liberty. Applicable whenever detention is illegal; can lie against private persons. Mandamus "We command" Public officials, Statutory bodies, Inferior Courts, Tribunals, Government Compel performance of a mandatory public or legal duty that has been refused/neglected. Does NOT lie against purely private bodies (unless discharging public duty) or President/Governors. Prohibition "To forbid" / "To restrain" Judicial and Quasi-Judicial bodies ONLY Prevent an inferior court/tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction or usurping Preventive stage -- Issued while the proceeding is still pending in the lower

Writ Name Literal Latin Meaning Primary Target / Body Core Objective / Purpose Procedural Stage jurisdiction not vested in it. body. Certiorari "To be certified" / "To be informed" Judicial, Quasi- Judicial (& administrative) bodies Quash an illegal order already passed due to lack/excess of jurisdiction or error of law on the face of the record. Curative stage -- Issued after an order/decision is made ("postmortem" review). Quo- Warranto "By what authority / warrant?" Person holding or claiming a substantive public office Prevent illegal usurpation of a permanent public office created by statute/Constitution. Can be moved by any public-minded citizen (does not require aggrieved party status). Crucial Distinctions  Prohibition vs Certiorari: o Prohibition: Issued to PREVENT -- Operates while the judicial/quasi-judicial proceeding is pending to halt excess of jurisdiction. o Certiorari: Issued to CORRECT/QUASH -- Operates after the order has been passed to remove or quash decisions suffering from jurisdictional error.  Habeas Corpus vs Mandamus: o Habeas Corpus targets illegal custody of a Person (remedy for bodily freedom). o Mandamus targets non-performance of a Legal Duty by a public authority.  Mandamus vs Quo-Warranto: o Mandamus commands: "Perform your lawful public duty." o Quo-Warranto challenges: "Show your legal qualification/title to hold this public office."

Imp Facts  Private Individuals: Habeas Corpus is the only writ directly applicable against private individuals in cases of illegal confinement.  Government Companies (IAS Trap): Mandamus can lie against a government company or statutory corporation performing a public function.  Locus Standi Exception: In Quo-Warranto, any member of the public can file a petition (traditional locus standi is relaxed; the petitioner does not need to be personally aggrieved).

x: The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on 9 December 1946.
Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the Objective Resolution on 13 December 1946.
The Objective Resolution was unanimously adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947.
The National Flag was adopted on 22 July 1947.
The Drafting Committee was constituted on 29 August 1947.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar headed the Drafting Committee.
The Constitution of India was adopted and enacted on 26 November 1949.
26 November is observed as Constitution Day.
The final meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on 24 January 1950.
The National Anthem was adopted on 24 January 1950.
The Constitution fully came into force on 26 January 1950.
The Republic of India was established on 26 January 1950.
The Regulating Act was enacted in 1773.
The Regulating Act changed the Governor of Bengal into the Governor-General of Bengal.
The Regulating Act provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
The Supreme Court at Calcutta was established in 1774.
Pitt’s India Act was enacted in 1784.
Pitt’s India Act introduced Dual Control.
The Board of Control handled political affairs under Dual Control.
The Court of Directors handled commerce under Dual Control.
The Charter Act was enacted in 1813.
The Charter Act of 1813 ended the trade monopoly in India.
The Charter Act of 1813 retained the trade monopoly in tea and China trade.
The Charter Act of 1813 provided an annual education grant of ₹1 lakh.
The Charter Act was enacted in 1833.
The Charter Act of 1833 created the office of Governor-General of India.
Bentinck was the Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833.
The Charter Act of 1833 added a Law Member.
Macaulay was the Law Member added under the Charter Act of 1833.
The Charter Act of 1833 ended the commercial role of the Governor-General of India.
The Charter Act was enacted in 1853.
The Charter Act of 1853 separated executive and legislative functions.
The Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competition for the Civil Services.
The Government of India Act was enacted in 1858.
The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred power to the British Crown.
The Government of India Act of 1858 created the office of Viceroy.
Canning was the Viceroy created under the Government of India Act of 1858.
The Indian Councils Act was enacted in 1861.
The Indian Councils Act of 1861 introduced the Portfolio System.
The Indian Councils Act of 1861 gave the Viceroy ordinance-making power.
The Indian Councils Act of 1861 restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras.
The Indian Councils Act was enacted in 1892.
The Indian Councils Act of 1892 permitted discussion of the budget.
The Indian Councils Act of 1892 introduced the principle of limited indirect election.
The Morley-Minto Reforms were introduced in 1909.
The Morley-Minto Reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
The Morley-Minto Reforms provided the first Indian member of the Executive Council.
S.P. Sinha was the first Indian in the Executive Council.
The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms were introduced in 1919.
The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms introduced bicameralism at the Centre.
The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms introduced direct elections at the Centre.
The Government of India Act was enacted in 1935.
The Government of India Act of 1935 introduced provincial autonomy.
The Government of India Act of 1935 proposed Central Dyarchy.
The Government of India Act of 1935 created the Federal Court.
The Federal Court was established on 1 October 1937.
The Indian Independence Act was enacted in 1947.
The Indian Independence Act ended British rule.
The Indian Independence Act created two independent Dominions.
The two independent Dominions were India and Pakistan.
The First Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 1951.
The First Constitutional Amendment Act added the Ninth Schedule.
The First Constitutional Amendment Act added Articles 31A and 31B.
The First Constitutional Amendment Act added Article 15(4).
The First Constitutional Amendment Act addressed agrarian reforms.
The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 1976.
The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act is known as the Mini-Constitution.
The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act added the terms Socialist, Secular and Integrity.
The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act added Part IVA.
Part IVA contains Article 51A.
The Forty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 1978.
The Forty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act removed the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights.
The Right to Property is provided under Article 300A.
The Forty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act inserted the term armed rebellion.
The Fifty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 1985.
The Fifty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act introduced the Anti-Defection Law.
The Anti-Defection Law is contained in the Tenth Schedule.
The Sixty-First Constitutional Amendment Act is associated with 1988/89.

The reduction of the voting age became effective on 28 March 1989.

The Eleventh Schedule is associated with Panchayats.
The Seventy-Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act introduced Municipalities.

The Twelfth Schedule is associated with Municipalities.
The Panchayat provisions were enforced on 24 April 1993.
The Municipality provisions were enforced on 1 June 1993.
The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 2002.
The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act added Article 21A.
Article 21A provides the Right to Education for children aged 6–14 years.
The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act added Article 51A(k).
The Ninety-First Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 2003.
The Ninety-First Constitutional Amendment Act capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the strength of the House.
The Ninety-Ninth Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 2014.
The Ninety-Ninth Constitutional Amendment Act introduced the National Judicial Appointments Commission.
The National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down in 2015.
The One Hundred and First Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 2016.
The One Hundred and First Constitutional Amendment Act introduced the Goods and Services Tax.

The One Hundred and Third and One Hundred and Fourth Constitutional Amendment Acts were enacted in 2019.
The One Hundred and Third Constitutional Amendment Act provided 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections.
The One Hundred and Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act ended Anglo-Indian nominations.

The One Hundred and Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 2023.
The One Hundred and Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act provided approximately one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was established in 1957.
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended a three-tier model.
Panchayati Raj was first launched on 2 October 1959.
Panchayati Raj was first launched at Nagaur in Rajasthan.
The Ashok Mehta Committee was established in 1977.
The G.V.K. Rao Committee was established in 1985.
The L.M. Singhvi Committee was established in 1986.
The provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act were enacted in 1996.

The Protection of Civil Rights Act was enacted in 1955.
The Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act was enacted in 1986.
The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was enacted in 1989.
The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was enforced on 30 January 1990.
The Protection of Human Rights Act was enacted in 1993.
The Protection of Human Rights Act was enforced on 28 September 1993.
The National Human Rights Commission was established on 12 October 1993.
The Right to Information Act was enacted in 2005.
The Right to Information Act was enforced on 12 October 2005.
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was enacted in 2005.
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was enforced on 26 October 2006.
The National Green Tribunal Act was enacted in 2010.
The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act was enacted in 2013.
The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act came into effect in 2014.

Years & Chronology Constitution-Making Timeline (1946–1950)  9 December 1946: First meeting of the Constituent Assembly.  13 December 1946: Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the Objective Resolution.  22 January 1947: Objective Resolution unanimously adopted by the Assembly.  22 July 1947: National Flag adopted.  29 August 1947: Drafting Committee constituted under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.  26 November 1949: Constitution of India adopted and enacted (Constitution Day).  24 January 1950: Final meeting of the Constituent Assembly; National Anthem adopted.  26 January 1950: Constitution fully came into force; Republic of India established. Constitutional Development & British Acts (1773–1947) Year British Act / Milestone Landmark Event / Signature Feature 1773 Regulating Act, 1773 Governor of Bengal  Governor-General of Bengal; Supreme Court at Calcutta provided (Est. 1774) 1784 Pitt’s India Act, 1784 Introduced Dual Control (Board of Control for politics + Court of Directors for commerce) 1813 Charter Act, 1813 Ended trade monopoly in India (except Tea & China trade); ₹1 Lakh annual education grant 1833 Charter Act, 1833 Governor-General of India (Bentinck); Law Member added (Macaulay); lost commercial role 1853 Charter Act, 1853 Separation of Executive & Legislative functions; Open Competition for Civil Services 1858 GoI Act, 1858 Transfer of power to the British Crown; created Viceroy (Canning) & Secretary of State

Year British Act / Milestone Landmark Event / Signature Feature 1861 Indian Councils Act, 1861 Portfolio System; Viceroy’s Ordinance power; restored Bombay/Madras legislative powers 1892 Indian Councils Act, 1892 Budget discussion permitted; limited indirect election principle 1909 Morley-Minto Reforms Separate Electorate for Muslims; first Indian in Executive Council (S.P. Sinha) 1919 Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms Dyarchy in Provinces; Bicameralism & Direct Elections at Centre 1935 Government of India Act, 1935 Provincial Autonomy; proposed Central Dyarchy; Federal Court created (Est. 1 Oct 1937) 1947 Indian Independence Act, 1947 Ended British rule; created two independent Dominions (India & Pakistan) Landmark Amendments, Local Self-Government & Governance Acts Key Constitutional Amendments: o 1951 (1st CAA): 9th Schedule, Arts. 31A, 31B, 15(4) (Agrarian reforms). o 1976 (42nd CAA): "Mini-Constitution"; added Socialist, Secular, Integrity; Part IVA (Art. 51A). o 1978 (44th CAA): Removed Right to Property from FRs (Art. 300A); "Armed rebellion" inserted. o 1985 (52nd CAA): Anti-Defection Law (10th Schedule). o 1988/89 (61st CAA): Voting age reduced from 21 to 18 years (effective 28 March 1989). o 1992 (73rd & 74th CAAs): Panchayats (Part IX, 11th Sched.) & Municipalities (Part IXA, 12th Sched.) (Enforced: 24 April 1993 & 1 June 1993). o 2002 (86th CAA): Added Art. 21A (Right to Education 6–14 yrs) & Art. 51A(k). o 2003 (91st CAA): Capped Council of Ministers at 15% of House strength. o 2014 (99th CAA): NJAC (Struck down in 2015).

o 2016 (101st CAA): Goods and Services Tax (GST, effective 1 July 2017). o 2019 (103rd & 104th CAAs): 10% EWS reservation; ended Anglo-Indian nominations (effective Jan 2020). o 2023 (106th CAA): ~1/3rd Women Reservation in Lok Sabha & State Assemblies. Evolution of Panchayati Raj & Decentralization: o 1957: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (3-tier model) -- 2 Oct 1959: First launched in Nagaur, Rajasthan. o 1977: Ashok Mehta Committee -- 1985: G.V.K. Rao Committee -- 1986: L.M. Singhvi Committee. o 1996: Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act (PESA). Major Governance & Social Welfare Statutes: o 1955: Protection of Civil Rights Act | 1986: Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act o 1989: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (Enforced: 30 January 1990) o 1993: Protection of Human Rights Act (Enforced: 28 September 1993; NHRC established 12 October 1993) o 2005: Right to Information (RTI) Act (Enforced: 12 October 2005) o 2005: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (Enforced: 26 October 2006) o 2010: National Green Tribunal (NGT) Act o 2013: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act (Came into effect in 2014)

Council  The term "Council" in Indian Polity spans three distinct constitutional institutions: o Council of Ministers (Union & State): Executive body aiding and advising the President/Governor. o Council of States (Rajya Sabha): Upper House of the Union Parliament (Art. 80). o State Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad): Upper House of bicameral State Legislatures (Arts. 168, 169, 171).  Parliamentary Components: Parliament consists of President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha (The Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha, but is NOT a constituent member of Parliament). Council of Ministers (Union vs State) Feature Union Council of Ministers State Council of Ministers Constitutional Basis Article 74 (Aid & advise President) Article 163 (Aid & advise Governor) Collective Responsibility Article 75(3) -- Strictly to Lok Sabha Article 164(2) -- Strictly to Legislative Assembly Individual Responsibility Pleasure of the President (NOT the PM) Pleasure of the Governor (NOT the CM) Size Limit (91st CAA, 2003) Max 15% of Lok Sabha total strength Max 15% of Legislative Assembly strength; Min: 12 Ministers Non-Member Tenure Max 6 consecutive months (Art. 75(5)) Max 6 consecutive months (Art. 164(4)) Cabinet vs Council Cabinet is the smaller inner core (PM + Cabinet Ministers); "Cabinet" inserted Inner core (CM + Cabinet Ministers)

Feature Union Council of Ministers State Council of Ministers into Art. 352 by 44th CAA, 1978 Reconsideration Power President can return advice once (44th CAA, 1978); bound thereafter Governor bound by ministerial advice except in discretionary areas Council of States (Rajya Sabha) — Art. 80  Nature: Permanent House; NOT subject to dissolution; 1/3rd of members retire every 2 years.  Member Tenure & Age: Member's term is 6 years; minimum age is 30 years.  Strength Limits: Maximum sanctioned strength = 250 members (238 representing States/UTs + 12 nominated by the President for expertise in Literature, Science, Art, and Social Service).  Electoral System: State representatives are elected by the elected MLAs of State Legislative Assemblies via Proportional Representation by Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV) under secret ballot (Nominated MLAs cannot vote). State Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)  Creation & Abolition (Art. 169): Initiated by the State Assembly passing a resolution by Special Majority (majority of total membership + ≥2/3rd present and voting) -- enacted into law by Parliament by Simple Majority.  Strength Limits (Art. 171): o Maximum Strength: 1/3rd of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly. o Minimum Strength: 40 members.  Composition Breakdown (Art. 171(3)): o 1/3rd elected by MLAs | 1/3rd elected by Local Authorities (Municipalities/District Boards) o 1/12th elected by Graduates (3+ yrs) | 1/12th elected by Teachers (3+ yrs) o 1/6th nominated by the Governor (Literature, Science, Art, Co-operative Movement, Social Service).

Comparison: State Legislative Assembly vs Legislative Council Feature Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) Chamber Type Lower / Popular House Upper House / House of Elders Nature & Term Dissolvable; 5-year term Permanent Body; 6-year member term Minimum Age 25 Years 30 Years Money Bill Role Sole House of introduction; Final authority Recommendatory only; Max detention: 14 days Ordinary Bill Delay Originating / Overriding Chamber Max 4 months (3 months 1st time + 1 month 2nd time) Presiding Officer Speaker (Decides Money Bill status) Chairman Imp Facts  Collective Responsibility Trap: Ministers are collectively responsible ONLY to the Lower House (Art. 75(3) to Lok Sabha; Art. 164(2) to Legislative Assembly)—NOT to the Rajya Sabha, Parliament as a whole, or the President/Governor.  Pleasure of Office: Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President / Governor, NOT the pleasure of the Prime Minister / Chief Minister.  Ordinary Bill Delay: Legislative Council cannot veto or permanently block an ordinary Bill passed by the Assembly; it can only delay it for a maximum of 4 months (3 + 1 months).

Union Minister  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V (Articles 74, 75, 77, 78); the Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head aids and advises the President of India.  Appointment (Art. 75(1)): Prime Minister is appointed by the President; other Union Ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.  Tenure (Art. 75(2)): Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President (Trap: Legally holds office during the pleasure of the President, NOT the Prime Minister).  Oath: The President administers both the Oath of Office and Oath of Secrecy under the Third Schedule.  Executive Head vs Head of State: Executive power is constitutionally vested in the President (Head of State) under Art. 53; the Prime Minister is the Head of Government. Membership & Parliamentary Rights (Art. 75(5) & Art. 88)  House Membership: A Union Minister can be a member of either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (No requirement to be a Lok Sabha member).  Non-Member Ministers: A person who is not a member of either House can be appointed as a Minister, but must become a member within 6 consecutive months; otherwise, ceases to be a Minister (Art. 75(5)).  Speaking vs Voting Rights (Art. 88 Trap): o Right to speak and participate in proceedings of both Houses & Joint Sittings -- YES o Right to vote in the House of which the Minister is NOT a member -- NO (Can vote ONLY in the House where they hold membership). Comparison: Council of Ministers vs Cabinet Feature Council of Ministers (CoM) Union Cabinet Body Size & Structure Wider constitutional body (60–80 members) Smaller, compact inner policy- making core (15–20 members) Composition PM + Cabinet Ministers + MoS (Independent) + MoS + Deputy Ministers Prime Minister + Cabinet Rank Ministers ONLY Constitutional Vested with broad powers under Original text lacked the word;

Feature Council of Ministers (CoM) Union Cabinet Mention Articles 74 & 75 inserted into Article 352(3) by 44th CAA, 1978 Four-Tier Classification Practical convention/tradition; NOT classified by the Constitution Highest executive category within the ranking hierarchy Functions Collective constitutional entity Core decision-making and apex policy formulation body Responsibility Framework & Size Limits  Collective Responsibility (Art. 75(3)): o The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible ONLY to the Lok Sabha (NOT to the Rajya Sabha, Parliament as a whole, or the President). o If the government loses a vote of confidence/majority in Lok Sabha, the entire Council must resign ("Sink or swim together").  Individual Responsibility: Ministers are answerable to Parliament for administrative/bureaucratic lapses under their respective portfolios.  15% Ceiling Limit (91st CAA, 2003): o Union (Art. 75(1A)): Total number of Union Ministers, including the PM, cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. o State Parallel (Art. 164(1A)): Cannot exceed 15% of the Legislative Assembly strength; minimum floor is 12 Ministers. Imp:  Prime Minister's Duties (Art. 78): PM communicates all decisions and administrative proposals to the President and submits any matter decided by an individual minister for Council consideration if required by the President.  Confidence vs No-Confidence Motion: o Confidence Motion: Moved on the floor by the Council of Ministers/Government to demonstrate majority. o No-Confidence Motion: Moved by the Opposition in the Lok Sabha (Rule 198).  Deputy Prime Minister Post: An extra-constitutional / non-constitutional post created for political convenience; carries the status of a Cabinet Minister without superior prime-ministerial powers (First Deputy PM: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, 1947–1950).

Collegium System  Core Mandate: The institutional system governing the appointment and transfer of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.  Origin & Status: It is NOT a constitutional body (not expressly mentioned in the Constitution) and was NOT created by an Act of Parliament—it is a judicially evolved system developed through Supreme Court rulings.  Appointing Authority (Art. 124(2) & 217(1)): Judges are formally appointed by the President of India based on the binding recommendations of the Collegium.  Functional Scope: Covers both Appointments (Supreme Court & High Courts) and Transfers (High Court Judges). Evolution: The Three Judges Cases Chain  First Judges Case (1981 – S.P. Gupta v. Union of India): Held that "consultation" does NOT mean "concurrence"; established Executive primacy in judicial appointments.  Second Judges Case (1993 – SCAORA v. Union of India): Reversed the 1981 ruling; held that "consultation" means concurrence; established Judicial primacy and formally birthed the Collegium system (1993).  Third Judges Case (1998 – Presidential Reference): Clarified procedural working; established that the CJI's opinion must reflect a plural consultation with senior colleagues (expanded the SC Collegium). Comparison: Collegium System vs NJAC Feature Collegium System (Current) NJAC (99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014) Legal Basis Judicially evolved through Supreme Court case law Enacted via 99th CAA, 2014 & NJAC Act, 2014 Total Strength 5 Members (for SC appointments) 6 Members Composition CJI + 4 senior-most Supreme Court Judges • CJI (Chairperson)

Feature Collegium System (Current) NJAC (99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014) • 2 Senior SC Judges • Union Law Minister • 2 Eminent Persons (nominated by PM + CJI + LoP) Executive Presence Zero executive representation Law Minister was a permanent member Judicial Outcome Restored and operational since 2015 Struck down as unconstitutional in 2015 (4th Judges Case) for violating Independence of the Judiciary Collegium Composition: Supreme Court vs High Courts  Supreme Court Appointments & Elevations: CJI + 4 Senior-most SC Judges (Total = 5 members).  High Court Appointments: Recommendation initiated by the Chief Justice of the HC + 2 senior-most HC judges -- forwarded to the Supreme Court Collegium (CJI + 2 Senior- most SC Judges).  High Court Transfers: Requisite consultation involves CJI + 4 Senior-most SC Judges + Chief Justices of both High Courts (transferring and receiving). Imp:  Origin & Statutory Traps: o Statement claiming "Parliament created the Collegium by law" -- FALSE (Judicially created). o Statement claiming "Collegium is expressly mentioned in Article 124" -- FALSE  Functional Scope Trap: The Collegium deals with Appointments AND Transfers (NOT appointments alone).  NJAC Striking Down Grounds: Struck down in 2015 because executive involvement infringed upon the Independence of the Judiciary, which is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

Institutional Governance & Governor's Special Powers  Tribal Advisory Council (TAC): Mandatory advisory body established in each State having Scheduled Areas (under Paragraph 4 of the Fifth Schedule) to advise on matters pertaining to the welfare and advancement of Scheduled Tribes.  Governor's Annual Report: The Governor submits a report regarding the administration of Scheduled Areas directly to the President of India (annually or whenever required by the President). o Trap: It is submitted by the Governor to the President, NOT by the Chief Minister to the Union Home Ministry.  Protection of Tribal Land (Paragraph 5): The Governor is empowered to make regulations prohibiting or restricting the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals and regulating money-lending to STs.  Samatha v. It does NOT apply to Manipur or Nagaland.  Declaring vs Reporting Authority: o Area Notification -- President o Administrative Report Submission -- Governor  President  Fifth vs Sixth Terminology: o Fifth Schedule = Scheduled Areas o Sixth Schedule = Tribal Areas

Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under any circumstances under Article 359.

The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 guaranteed that enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Article 359.

Article 360 has never been invoked in India since independence.

Emergency Provisions  Constitutional Placement: Governed under Part XVIII (Articles 352–360).  Three Classifications: o Article 352: National Emergency (War, External Aggression, Armed Rebellion). o Article 356: President's Rule (Failure of Constitutional Machinery in a State). o Article 360: Financial Emergency (Threat to financial stability or credit of India).  Philosophical Critique: K.M. Nambiar characterized the President’s emergency powers as a "fraud on the Constitution". Comparison: Three Types of Emergencies Feature National Emergency (Art. 352) President's Rule (Art. 356) Financial Emergency (Art. 360) Grounds War, External Aggression, or Armed Rebellion Failure of constitutional machinery (Governor's report or otherwise) Threat to financial stability or credit of India / any part Approval Timeframe 1 Month (Reduced from 2 months by 44th CAA) 2 Months 2 Months Majority Required Special Majority in both Houses Simple Majority in both Houses Simple Majority in both Houses Continuation Period 6 Months at a time (No maximum limit) 6 Months at a time (Maximum 3 Years) Continues until revoked by President Dissolved Lok Sabha Survives for 30 Days from 1st sitting of new LS Survives for 30 Days from 1st sitting of new LS Survives for 30 Days from 1st sitting of new LS

Feature National Emergency (Art. 352) President's Rule (Art. 356) Financial Emergency (Art. 360) Impact on State Powers Parliament can make laws on the State List State Assembly dissolved/suspended; Parliament passes State Budget Executive gives financial directions; can reduce salaries (including SC/HC Judges) Impact on FRs Arts. 358 & 359 operate; Arts. 20 & 21 can NEVER be suspended No direct suspension of Fundamental Rights No direct suspension of Fundamental Rights Times Invoked in India 3 Times (1962, 1971, 1975) Invoked over 100 times across various States NEVER Invoked (0 Times) National Emergency: Legislative & Financial Mechanisms  Term Extension of Legislatures: o Lok Sabha & State Assemblies: Parliament can extend their terms by law for 1 year at a time, up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases.  Laws on State List Subjects: Parliament acquires overriding legislative jurisdiction over State List subjects; such laws cease to operate 6 months after the Emergency is revoked.  Modifying Revenue Distribution (Art. 354): The President is empowered to modify the constitutional distribution of revenues between the Union and States (valid up to the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases).

Effect on Fundamental Rights: Article 358 vs Article 359 Feature Article 358 (Suspension of Art. 19 Freedoms) Article 359 (Suspension of Right to Move Courts) Scope of Rights Automatically suspends the 6 basic freedoms under Article 19 Suspends the right to approach courts for enforcement of specified FRs Applicable Grounds Operates ONLY on grounds of War or External Aggression (External Emergency) Operates on both External Emergency AND Internal Emergency (Armed Rebellion) Automatic Nature Automatic suspension upon proclamation Requires a specific, separate Presidential Order Non-Suspendable Exception Does not operate during an "Armed Rebellion" proclamation Articles 20 & 21 CANNOT be suspended under any circumstances (44th CAA) President's Rule (Art. 356) & Beyond 1-Year Conditions  Invocation Basis: Imposed when the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution; the President may act on a report from the Governor OR suo motu (otherwise).  Conditions for Extension Beyond 1 Year (Up to 3-Year Cap): 1. A National Emergency is in operation in the whole of India or in any part of the State, AND 2. The Election Commission of India certifies that general elections to the State Assembly cannot be held. Imp Facts  44th Amendment Act, 1978 Landmarks: o Replaced "Internal Disturbance" with "Armed Rebellion" under Article 352. o Reduced parliamentary approval time for National Emergency from 2 months to 1 month. o Guaranteed that the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 can NEVER be suspended under Article 359.

o Added requirement that the President can proclaim National Emergency only upon written advice of the Union Cabinet.  1975 Emergency Timeline: Proclaimed on 25 June 1975 (on ground of Internal Disturbance) and formally withdrawn on 21 March 1977.  Financial Emergency Trap: Article 360 has NEVER been invoked in India since independence.

x: Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments.

The Supreme Court exercises Judicial Review under Article 32.
The High Courts exercise Judicial Review under Article 226.
Judicial Review is vested jointly in the Supreme Court and the High Courts.
Judicial Review is not vested in the Supreme Court alone.
India adopted Judicial Review from the United States of America.
Judicial Review originated in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.
Chief Justice John Marshall was associated with the origin of Judicial Review in Marbury v. Madison.
India follows constitutional supremacy with Judicial Review.
The United Kingdom follows parliamentary sovereignty.
The United Kingdom has no traditional Judicial Review of primary parliamentary legislation.
Article 13(2) is the primary textual foundation of Judicial Review.
Article 13(2) provides that laws abridging Fundamental Rights are void pro tanto.
Article 13(2) is an express constitutional basis for striking down ultra vires laws.
Article 32 provides the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Article 32 is a constitutional remedy.
Article 32 is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
Article 226 provides the High Courts' writ jurisdiction for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Article 226 also covers the enforcement of any other legal right.
Article 226 has a wider writ scope than Article 32.
Article 137 gives the Supreme Court the power to review its own judgments or orders.
Article 137 provides for review of the Supreme Court's own judgment.
Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass decrees or orders for Complete Justice.
Article 142 represents inherent equitable jurisdiction.
Article 142 is distinct from Judicial Review.
In Kesavananda Bharati in 1973, Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was declared an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
Minerva Mills in 1980 reaffirmed that Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 is an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
Parliament cannot abrogate Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 even through Article 368.
Constitutional amendments are subject to Judicial Review on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine.
The First Constitutional Amendment Act of 1951 added Articles 31A and 31B.
The First Constitutional Amendment Act of 1951 added the Ninth Schedule.
Articles 31A, 31B, and the Ninth Schedule were added to insulate agrarian laws from Judicial Review on Fundamental Rights grounds.
Articles 31A, 31B, and the Ninth Schedule were added to insulate land-reform laws from Judicial Review on Fundamental Rights grounds.
The Ninth Schedule was enacted largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting state welfare measures.
The Ninth Schedule was enacted largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting land acquisition measures.
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the political wisdom of legislation.
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the policy merits of legislation.
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the advisability of legislation.
Judicial Review is not automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills.
Judicial Review is not an ordinary appellate proceeding.
Judicial Review reinforces the federal principle.
Judicial Review preserves the constitutional distribution of powers.
Judicial Review enforces constitutional limits.
Judicial Review is not a unitary element.
All India Services are a unitary element.
The Governor's appointment is a unitary element.
Emergency provisions are unitary elements.

Judicial Review  Definition: The inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders, declaring them void if they contravene constitutional provisions.  Exercising Authority: Vested jointly in the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226) (NOT the Supreme Court alone).  Borrowed Source: Adopted from the USA (originated in Marbury v. Madison, 1803 by Chief Justice John Marshall).  Constitutional Supremacy vs. Parliamentary Sovereignty: o India: Constitutional Supremacy with Judicial Review. o UK: Parliamentary Sovereignty (No traditional judicial review of primary parliamentary legislation). Constitutional Bases & Distinct Article Provisions Article Constitutional Domain & Significance Note Article 13(2) Primary textual foundation; laws abridging Fundamental Rights are void pro tanto Express constitutional basis for striking down ultra vires laws Article 32 Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights enforcement Constitutional remedy & part of the Basic Structure Article 226 High Court writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights + any other legal right Wider writ scope than Article 32 Article 137 Supreme Court's power to review its own judgments or orders Judicial Review - Art. 137 Review (Review of own judgment) Article 142 Power of Supreme Court to pass decrees/orders for "Complete Justice" Inherent equitable jurisdiction (Distinct from Judicial Review)

Judicial Review, Basic Structure & 9th Schedule  Basic Structure Integration: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and reaffirmed in Minerva Mills (1980), Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was declared an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution; Parliament cannot abrogate it even via Article 368.  Review of Constitutional Amendments: Constitutional amendments are themselves subject to Judicial Review on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine.  The 9th Schedule Shield (1st CAA, 1951): o Added Articles 31A, 31B, and the 9th Schedule to insulate agrarian and land- reform laws from judicial review on Fundamental Rights grounds. o Enacted largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting state welfare/land acquisition measures. Imp  What Judicial Review is NOT: o It is NOT the court questioning the political wisdom, policy merits, or advisability of legislation. o It is NOT automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills. o It is NOT an ordinary appellate proceeding.  Federal vs. Unitary Classification Trap: o Judicial Review reinforces the Federal principle (preserves constitutional distribution of powers and enforces constitutional limits). o It is NOT a Unitary element (unlike All India Services, Governor's appointment, or emergency provisions).

Representation of the People Acts (RPA 1950 & 1951)  Key Distinction: o RPA, 1950: Deals with the allocation of seats, delimitation of constituencies, voter qualifications, preparation of electoral rolls, and the detailed composition of State Legislative Councils (Art. 171(2)  ↔ Section 10 & 3rd Schedule of RPA 1950). o RPA, 1951: Deals with the actual conduct of elections, qualifications/disqualifications of candidates, registration of political parties, corrupt practices, election petitions, and disputes.  Party Registration & Recognition: Political parties are registered by the Election Commission of India (ECI) under Section 29A of RPA 1951; recognized as National/State parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 (NOT by Parliament, Law Ministry, or President).  Right to Vote & Right to Contest: Established as Legal / Statutory Rights (Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India, 2006), NOT Fundamental Rights.

Comparison: RPA 1950 vs RPA 1951 Feature Representation of the People Act, 1950 Representation of the People Act, 1951 Primary Scope Pre-election framework & voter rolls Operational conduct of elections & candidature Constituency Allocation Allocation of Lok Sabha, Assembly & Council seats Nomination, scrutiny & counting procedures Electoral Rolls Registration of electors & preparation of rolls Disqualifications for holding membership Key Operational Provisions Seat quotas, Delimitation framework Political party registration (Sec. 29A), Corrupt practices
Feature Representation of the People Act, 1950 Representation of the People Act, 1951 Connected Constitutional Part Articles 81, 82, 170, 171, 325, 326 Articles 84, 102, 173, 191, 324, 329

Key Legislative Amendments & Candidature Rules  Section 33(7) of RPA, 1951 (Contesting Seat Limits): o A candidate can contest from a maximum of 2 Parliamentary or 2 Assembly constituencies at a time. o Origin & Context: Following the 1991 elections where Devi Lal contested from 3 Lok Sabha seats, RPA 1951 was amended in 1996 (capping the limit at 2).  Rajya Sabha Domicile / Voter Requirement (2003 Amendment): o Prior to 2003, a candidate contesting for Rajya Sabha had to be an elector in that particular State. o The 2003 Amendment removed this requirement; any registered elector in India can contest from any State. Upheld by the SC in Kuldip Nayar (2006).  Death of a Contesting Candidate (1996 Amendment): o Elections are no longer countermanded automatically upon the death of a candidate; recognized political parties are permitted to nominate a replacement within a set timeframe.  Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990): Set up on Electoral Reforms; recommended state funding of elections, EVMs, and the measures subsequently enacted in the 1996 RPA Amendment.

Delimitation Commission & Electoral Technology  Delimitation Commission: o Constituted by the Central Government under an Act of Parliament (headed by a retired SC Judge + CEC + State SECs). o Finality of Orders: Orders have the force of law and cannot be called in question in any court (Art. 329). When laid before Parliament/Assemblies, orders cannot be modified. o Four Delimitation Commissions constituted so far: 1952, 1963, 1973, and 2002.

o VVPAT First Use: Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland (September 2013). o NOTA Introduction: Directed by Supreme Court on 27 September 2013 (PUCL v. Union of India). Imp  Party Registration Authority: Always eliminate options attributing political party registration to the Ministry of Law & Justice or Parliament It is strictly executed by the Election Commission of India (ECI).  National Party Criteria:  A political party must win at least 6% of the total valid votes in four or more states during a Lok Sabha (Lok Sabha general election) or State Legislative Assembly election, AND it must also win at least 4 Lok Sabha seats from any state or states.  Alternatively, a party must win at least 2% of the total seats in the Lok Sabha (which equals 11 seats), and these elected members must come from at least 3 different states.  Alternatively, a party must be officially recognized as a State Party in at least 4 different states.
 Model Code of Conduct (MCC): Comes into force immediately upon the formal announcement of the election schedule by the ECI.

Political Party Political Parties & Anti-Defection Dynamics (10th Schedule)  Merger Protection Exception: Disqualification on grounds of defection does not apply if a party merges with another and ≥ 2/3rd of the members of the legislative party agree to the merger (The original 1/3rd "split" exemption was omitted by the 91st CAA, 2003).  Scope of Disqualification: Applies to members voluntarily giving up party membership or voting/abstaining contrary to party whips without prior permission. Historical Timeline of Political Parties & Splits  1885: Indian National Congress (INC; First President: W.C. Banerjee).  1925: Communist Party of India (CPI).  1951: Bharatiya Jana Sangh (BJS; Founder: Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee).  1964: CPI Split -- Formation of Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)].  1980: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP; First President: Atal Bihari Vajpayee; successor to BJS).  1984: Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP).  1992: Samajwadi Party (SP).  1998: All India Trinamool Congress (AITC / TMC).  1999: Nationalist Congress Party (NCP; split from INC by Sharad Pawar, P.A. Sangma, Tariq Anwar). Key Political Science Concepts & Leader of Opposition (LoP)  "One-Party Dominant System" / "Congress System": Term coined by political scientist Rajni Kothari to characterize India's democratic, multi-party electoral landscape dominated by the Congress party post-independence.  End of the "Congress System": Marked by the 1989 General Election (ushering in the era of minority/coalition governments; V.P. Singh led National Front with outside support from BJP + Left).  Leader of Opposition (LoP) Recognition: o First formally recognized in 1969. o Numerical Threshold: The largest opposition party must hold ≥ 10% of the total House strength (approx 55 seats in Lok Sabha).
Traps:

 Merger Fraction Trap: Protection from defection requires agreement of 2/3rd members, NOT 1/3rd (1/3rd is the obsolete split threshold).  Constitutional Recognition: Parties were NOT part of the original 1950 text; introduced via 52nd CAA, 1985 (10th Schedule).  National Party Threshold: Requires ≥ 6% votes in 4 States + 4 Lok Sabha seats (both conditions mandatory under Route 2).

Three Budget Cut Motions (Demands for Grants)  Policy Cut Motion: Move to reduce the demand to ₹1 (Represents complete disapproval of the underlying policy).  Economy Cut Motion: Move to reduce the demand by a specified amount (Aims at achieving administrative economy).  Token Cut Motion: Move to reduce the demand by ₹100 (Ventilates a specific grievance within government responsibility).  Consequence: The passage of any Cut Motion in Lok Sabha signals loss of financial control and obliges the Government to resign. Special Rules & Miscellaneous Procedures  Rule 184 (Lok Sabha): Permits discussion on a matter of public interest accompanied by a formal motion and voting (If defeated, ruling party faces potential collapse).  Rule 377 (Lok Sabha): Allows members to raise urgent matters not covered under Questions, Calling Attention, or other motions (Written notice to Secretary-General; raised from 20 to 30 matters/day in 2015).  Interpellation: The formal procedural right of asking questions to demand explanations of government actions or policies from the Executive.  Yielding the Floor: The parliamentary convention where the Speaker orders a speaking member to yield/stop to allow another member to speak. Imp  20: Maximum Starred Questions listed for oral answer per day.  30: Maximum matters allowed to be raised daily under Rule 377 (post-2015).  50: Minimum members required to support the admission of a No-Confidence Motion.  ₹1: Reduction amount in a Policy Cut Motion.  ₹100: Reduction amount in a Token Cut Motion.

 1 Hour: Maximum duration of Zero Hour in Lok Sabha.  11:00 AM – 12:00 Noon: Question Hour in Lok Sabha  ↔ Zero Hour in Rajya Sabha.  12:00 Noon – 1:00 PM: Zero Hour in Lok Sabha  ↔ Question Hour in Rajya Sabha (post- 2014).

Speaker of Lok Sabha  Constitutional Basis: Governed under Part V (Articles 93–96, 100, 110, 118); chosen/elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members (Art. 93).  Membership Requirement: Must already be an elected MP of Lok Sabha at the time of election (A non-member cannot be chosen as Speaker under the 6-month relaxation rule).  Oath of Office: The Speaker takes NO separate oath of office as presiding officer (Takes oath solely as an ordinary Member of Parliament).  Administrative Control: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions directly under the control and guidance of the Speaker. Comparison: Normal Floor Proceedings vs Own Removal Proceedings Procedural Parameter Normal Parliamentary Sittings During Consideration of Own Removal Resolution (Art. 96) Right to Preside YES (Presides over House proceedings) NO  (Cannot preside even if present in the House) Right to Speak / Participate YES YES (Has the right to speak and take part in proceedings) First-Instance Vote NO  (Does not vote in the first instance) YES (Entitled to vote in the first instance like an ordinary member) Casting Vote (Tie- Breaker) YES (Exercises casting vote under Art. 100 upon an equality of votes) NO (Cannot exercise a casting vote in case of a tie) Vacation, Resignation, Dissolution & Removal Rules  Resignation Route (Art. 94(b)): o Speaker addresses resignation in writing to the Deputy Speaker (Reciprocal: Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker). o Trap: Resignation goes across laterally, NOT upward to the President.  Effect of Dissolution (Universal Exception Trap):

o When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker does NOT vacate office immediately. o Continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Lok Sabha.  Removal Mechanism (Art. 94(c)): o Removed only by a resolution passed by a majority of ALL THE THEN MEMBERS of the Lok Sabha (Effective Majority). o Requires at least 14 days' advance written notice before moving the resolution. Special Constitutional Powers & Functions  Money Bill Certification (Art. 110(4)): Sole and final authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill; endorsement is final when transmitted to Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.  Presiding over Joint Sittings (Art. 118(4)): Presides over joint sittings of both Houses of Parliament (In absence: Deputy Speaker Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha).  Maintenance of Order: Adjourns the House or suspends sittings in the absence of a Quorum (1/10th strength under Art. 100); exercises Adjournment Sine Die.  Anti-Defection Disqualifications: Decides questions of member disqualification arising out of defection under the 10th Schedule (Subject to judicial review per Kihoto Hollohan).  Fixing Deputy Speaker Election: The Speaker fixes the date for the election of the Deputy Speaker under Rule 8(1). Comparison: Regular Speaker vs Pro-Tem Speaker Feature Regular Speaker of Lok Sabha Pro-Tem Speaker Constitutional Basis Article 93 Article 95(1) (Convention/Practice) Selection / Appointing Mode Elected by Lok Sabha members Appointed by the President Eligibility Profile Sitting member of the House Usually the senior-most elected MP of the newly elected House Core Primary Regular presiding officer; Administers oath to newly elected MPs;

Feature Regular Speaker of Lok Sabha Pro-Tem Speaker Function enforces rules & business enables election of the regular Speaker Tenure Survives dissolution until next House meets Temporary; office ceases the moment the regular Speaker is elected Historical Milestones  First Speaker of Lok Sabha: G.V. Mavalankar (1952–1956).  First Woman Speaker: Meira Kumar (15th Lok Sabha, 2009–2014).  Second Woman Speaker: Sumitra Mahajan (16th Lok Sabha, 2014–2019).

Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V (Articles 93–96); chosen/elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members (Art. 93).  Election Date Authority (Rule 8(1)): The date of election of the Deputy Speaker is fixed by the Speaker of Lok Sabha (communicated to all members by the Secretary-General).  Constitutional Status vs Convention: o The Constitution does NOT mandate that the Deputy Speaker must belong to the Opposition. o Selection of the Deputy Speaker from the Opposition is a parliamentary convention/practice, NOT a mandatory constitutional requirement.  Oath of Office: Like the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker takes NO separate oath of office as presiding officer (takes oath solely as an ordinary MP). Direct Comparison: Speaker vs Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha Feature Speaker of Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha Constitutional Basis Article 93 Article 93 Election & Mode Elected by Lok Sabha from among its members Elected by Lok Sabha from among its members Election Date Decided By President fixes the election date Speaker fixes the election date (Rule 8(1)) Separate Oath of Office NO (Takes oath solely as MP) NO (Takes oath solely as MP) Resignation Addressed To Deputy Speaker (Art. 94(b)) Speaker (Art. 94(b)) Removal Authority & Notice Lok Sabha (Effective Majority; 14 days' notice) Lok Sabha (Effective Majority; 14 days' notice)

Feature Speaker of Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha Status during Own Removal Cannot preside; Can speak & vote in 1st instance (Art. 96) Cannot preside; Can speak & vote in 1st instance (Art. 96) Continuation after Dissolution Continues until 1st meeting of new Lok Sabha Vacates immediately upon cessation/dissolution Powers & Privileges While Presiding (Art. 95)  Equality of Powers: When presiding over a sitting of the Lok Sabha, the Deputy Speaker exercises the same powers as the Speaker.  Finality of Rulings: There is no appeal to the Speaker against any ruling given by the Deputy Speaker while in the Chair.  Joint Sittings (Art. 118(4)): Presides over Joint Sittings of Parliament if the Speaker is absent.  Parliamentary Committees: If appointed to any Parliamentary Committee, the Deputy Speaker automatically becomes its Chairman. Floor Rights: Normal Sittings vs Own Removal (Art. 96)  During Normal Proceedings (When NOT in the Chair): o Sits as an ordinary member of the House. o Can participate in debates, move motions, and vote in the first instance.  During Consideration of Own Removal Resolution (Art. 96): o Cannot preside over the sitting even if present in the House. o Has the right to speak, participate, and vote in the first instance. o Cannot exercise a casting vote in case of an equality of votes (tie). Imp  Lateral Resignation Trap: Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker, NOT to the President or Prime Minister.  Dissolution Protection Distinction: The special constitutional protection to continue holding office after the dissolution of Lok Sabha applies only to the Speaker, NOT the Deputy Speaker.  Removal Majority: Requires a majority of all the then members of Lok Sabha (Effective Majority), NOT a Simple Majority or 2/3rd Special Majority.

The Legislative Assembly is the base constitutional House for the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council.
Creation or abolition of a Legislative Council requires an Assembly special majority and a Parliamentary simple majority.
The general maximum strength of a State Legislative Assembly under Article 170 is 500 seats.
The general minimum strength of a State Legislative Assembly under Article 170 is 60 seats.
Uttar Pradesh has the largest State Legislative Assembly.
The Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly has 403 seats.
Sikkim has the smallest State Legislative Assembly.
The Sikkim Legislative Assembly has 32 seats.
The Goa Legislative Assembly has 40 seats.
The Mizoram Legislative Assembly has 40 seats.
Puducherry has the smallest Union Territory Assembly.
The Puducherry Assembly has 33 seats.
The Puducherry Assembly has 30 elected members.
The Puducherry Assembly has 3 nominated members.
Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes in every State Legislative Assembly in proportion to their population in the State.
Seats are reserved for Scheduled Tribes in every State Legislative Assembly in proportion to their population in the State.
Article 332 deals with reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in State Legislative Assemblies.
A State Money Bill can originate only in the Legislative Assembly on the Governor’s prior recommendation.
Article 207 deals with the Governor’s prior recommendation for State Money Bills.
The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly has sole and final authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
The Legislative Council must return a Money Bill within 14 days.
The Legislative Assembly may accept or reject the Legislative Council’s recommendations on a Money Bill.
When the Legislative Assembly passes an ordinary Bill and transmits it to the Legislative Council, the Council can delay it for up to three months in the first instance.
When the Legislative Assembly re-passes an ordinary Bill, the Legislative Council can delay it for up to one month in the second instance.
The total maximum delay of an ordinary Bill by the Legislative Council is four months.
The Legislative Council has no veto power over an ordinary Bill passed by the Legislative Assembly.
The Legislative Council cannot permanently block an ordinary Bill passed by the Legislative Assembly.
The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years under Article 172.
During a National Emergency under Article 352, Parliament may extend the Legislative Assembly’s duration by law for one year at a time.
The Legislative Assembly’s duration may be extended only up to six months after the National Emergency ceases.
The Governor summons the Legislative Assembly.
The Governor prorogues the Legislative Assembly.
The Governor dissolves the Legislative Assembly.
Article 174 deals with summoning, prorogation, and dissolution of the Legislative Assembly.
Holding an office of profit is a ground for disqualification from membership of the Legislative Assembly.
Unsoundness of mind is a ground for disqualification from membership of the Legislative Assembly.
Being an undischarged insolvent is a ground for disqualification from membership of the Legislative Assembly.
Loss of citizenship is a ground for disqualification from membership of the Legislative Assembly.
Article 191 specifies grounds for disqualification from membership of a State Legislature.
The Governor decides questions of disqualification under Article 192.
The Governor must obtain the opinion of the Election Commission of India on disqualification questions under Article 192.
The Governor must act according to the Election Commission of India’s opinion on disqualification questions.
An Assembly resolution recommending creation or abolition of a Legislative Council requires a special majority.
The special majority requires at least 50 percent of the total Assembly membership.
The special majority requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting.
An Assembly resolution recommending creation or abolition of a Legislative Council does not compel the Union Government to introduce a Bill in Parliament.
Andhra Pradesh has a Legislative Council.
Telangana has a Legislative Council.
Bihar has a Legislative Council.
Maharashtra has a Legislative Council.
Karnataka has a Legislative Council.
Uttar Pradesh has a Legislative Council.
The six States with Legislative Councils are Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Uttar Pradesh.
Disqualifications under Article 191 are decided by the Governor acting on the Election Commission of India’s binding advice.
The Speaker decides disqualification matters under the Tenth Schedule’s anti-defection provisions.

State Legislative Assembly  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part VI (Articles 168–212); the Legislative Assembly is the Lower / Popular House of the State Legislature (Art. 168).  State Legislature Composition (Art. 168): o Unicameral States: Governor + Legislative Assembly. o Bicameral States: Governor + Legislative Assembly + Legislative Council.  Electoral System: Directly elected by the people from single-member territorial constituencies based on Universal Adult Suffrage (Art. 326) using the First-Past-the- Post (FPTP) system conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI). o FPTP Trap: A candidate does NOT need an absolute majority (>50%); the candidate securing the highest number of valid votes wins.  Presiding Officers (Art. 178): Speaker and Deputy Speaker are chosen/elected by the Assembly from amongst its own sitting members. Comparison: State Legislative Assembly vs Legislative Council Feature Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) Constitutional Basis Article 170 Article 171 Chamber Nature & Term Dissolvable / Temporary; 5- Year Term Permanent Body; 1/3rd retire every 2 yrs (6-yr member term) Minimum Age (Art. 173) 25 Years 30 Years Maximum Strength 500 Members 1/3rd of total Assembly strength Minimum Strength 60 Members (subject to statutory exceptions) 40 Members Money Bill (Art. Introduced ONLY in Recommendatory only; Max detention:

Feature Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) 198/199) Assembly; Speaker certifies 14 Days Ordinary Bill Delay (Art. 197) Originating / Overriding Chamber Max 4 Months (3 Months 1st time + 1 Month 2nd time) Creation / Abolition Base constitutional House Article 169 (Assembly Special Majority + Parliament Simple Majority) Assembly Strength: Ceilings, Floors & Superlatives  General Limits (Art. 170): Maximum = 500 seats | Minimum = 60 seats.  Superlatives & Exceptions: o Largest State Assembly: Uttar Pradesh (403 seats). o Smallest State Assembly: Sikkim (32 seats) (Other small states: Goa = 40, Mizoram = 40). o Smallest UT Assembly: Puducherry (33 seats) (30 elected + 3 nominated).  SC/ST Seat Reservation (Art. 332): Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in every State Legislative Assembly in proportion to their population in the State. Legislative Powers: Money Bills vs Ordinary Bills  State Money Bills (Art. 198 & 199): o Can originate ONLY in the Legislative Assembly on the prior recommendation of the Governor (Art. 207). o The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly has sole and final authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill. o Legislative Council must return the Bill within 14 days; Assembly can accept or reject recommendations.  Ordinary Bills & Council Delay Power (Art. 197 Trap): o When an Assembly passes an ordinary Bill and transmits it to the Council:  First Instance: Council can delay up to 3 Months.  Second Instance (Re-passed by Assembly): Council can delay up to 1 Month. o Total Maximum Delay: 4 Months (3 + 1 Months). o Trap: The State Council has no veto power and cannot permanently block an ordinary Bill passed by the Assembly.

Tenure, Dissolution & Disqualification Mechanisms  Term & Emergency Extension (Art. 172): Normal term is 5 years; during a National Emergency (Art. 352), Parliament may extend the Assembly's duration by law for 1 year at a time, up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases.  Summoning & Dissolution (Art. 174): The Governor summons, prorogues, and dissolves the Legislative Assembly.  Member Disqualifications (Art. 191 & 192): o Grounds include holding an office of profit, unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, or loss of citizenship (Art. 191). o Deciding Authority (Art. 192): The Governor decides disqualification questions, but MUST obtain the opinion of the Election Commission of India (ECI) and act according to such opinion. Traps:  Article 169 Resolution Trap: An Assembly resolution recommending the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council requires a Special Majority (≥ 50 %total membership + ≥ 2/3 rdpresent and voting), but does NOT compel the Union Government to introduce a Bill in Parliament.  Bicameral States Snapshot (6 States): Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Uttar Pradesh.  Disqualification Deciding Head: Disqualifications under Art. 191 are decided by the Governor acting on ECI's binding advice (Anti-defection under 10th Schedule is decided by the Speaker).

x: The Consolidated Fund and financial funds are governed under Part XII of the Constitution.
Part XII covers Articles 265 to 267.
The Consolidated Fund and financial funds are governed under Part V of the Constitution.
Part V covers Articles 112 to 116.
The Consolidated Fund of India contains all revenues received by the Government.
Government revenues include taxes.
Government revenues include duties.
Government revenues include non-tax revenue.
The Consolidated Fund of India contains all loans raised by the Government.
Government loans include treasury bills.
Government loans include market loans.
Government loans include foreign loans.
The Consolidated Fund of India contains all money received in repayment of loans.
No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under appropriation made by a law passed by Parliament.
Article 114 provides the appropriation authority for withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India.
The President cannot authorize withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India on the President’s own authority.
The Prime Minister cannot authorize withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India on the Prime Minister’s own authority.
The Finance Minister cannot authorize withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India on the Finance Minister’s own authority.
The Comptroller and Auditor General cannot authorize withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India on the CAG’s own authority.
The Consolidated Fund of India is constituted under Article 266(1).
The Public Account of India is constituted under Article 266(2).
The Contingency Fund of India is constituted under Article 267(1).
The Public Account of India holds money in trust or custody.
Provident funds are held in the Public Account of India.
Judicial deposits are held in the Public Account of India.
Savings bank deposits are held in the Public Account of India.
The Contingency Fund of India is an imprest placed at the disposal of the President.
The Contingency Fund of India is used for unforeseen expenses.
The Parliament of India controls the Consolidated Fund of India.
The Executive or Government controls the Public Account of India.
The Public Account of India operates as a banker.
The President of India controls the Contingency Fund of India.
The Finance Secretary administers the Contingency Fund of India on behalf of the President.
Parliamentary approval through an Appropriation Act under Article 114 is mandatory for withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India.
Prior parliamentary voting is not required for executive disbursements from the Public Account of India.
Prior parliamentary voting is not required for advances from the Contingency Fund of India.
Ex-post facto approval is required later for advances from the Contingency Fund of India.
The Consolidated Fund of India is a dynamic main treasury account.
The Public Account of India is an operational banking account.
The Contingency Fund of India has a fixed statutory corpus.
Charged expenditure is non-votable expenditure.
Charged expenditure can be discussed by both Houses of Parliament.
Charged expenditure is not submitted to the vote of Parliament.
The Constitution guarantees charged expenditure to maintain the financial independence of constitutional offices.
The emoluments and allowances of the President are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The office expenses of the President are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salaries, allowances, and pensions of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salaries, allowances, and pensions of the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salaries, allowances, and pensions of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salaries, allowances, and pensions of the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salaries, allowances, and pensions of Supreme Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Only the pensions of High Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salary, allowances, and pension of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Debt charges for which the Government of India is liable are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Interest on government debt is a debt charge charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Sinking fund charges are debt charges charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Any sum required to satisfy a judgment against the Government of India is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Any sum required to satisfy a decree against the Government of India is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Any sum required to satisfy an arbitral award against the Government of India is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The Vice-President receives no salary as Vice-President.
The Vice-President’s salary is drawn in the capacity of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The salary of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salaries and allowances of the Prime Minister are votable.
The salaries and allowances of Union Ministers are votable.
The salaries and allowances of the Prime Minister and Union Ministers are not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salaries of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners are not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The administrative expenses of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners are not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
The salaries and allowances of High Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State under Article 202(3).
The pensions of High Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 112(3)(d)(iii).
The Governor’s emoluments are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
Article 265 provides that no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
Article 266 deals with the Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts of the Union and the States.
Article 267 deals with the Contingency Funds of the Union and the States.
Article 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement, or Union Budget.
Article 113 deals with the procedure in Parliament regarding estimates.
Demands for Grants are covered by Article 113.
Article 114 deals with Appropriation Bills.
Appropriation Bills provide authority for withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India.
Article 115 deals with supplementary grants.
Article 115 deals with additional grants.
Article 115 deals with excess grants.
Article 116 deals with the Vote on Account.
Article 116 deals with Votes of Credit.
Article 116 deals with Exceptional Grants.

Consolidated Fund & Financial Funds  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part XII (Articles 265–267) and Part V (Articles 112–116).  Composition of Consolidated Fund (Art. 266(1)): 1. All revenues received by the Government (taxes, duties, non-tax revenue). 2. All loans raised by the Government (treasury bills, market loans, foreign loans). 3. All moneys received in repayment of loans.  Withdrawal Authority (Universal Rule): No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under appropriation made by law passed by Parliament (Article 114 – Appropriation Act). o Trap: Neither the President, Prime Minister, Finance Minister, nor the CAG can authorize withdrawals from the CFI on their own authority. Comparison: Three Constitutional Funds Feature Consolidated Fund of India (CFI) Public Account of India Contingency Fund of India Constitutional Article Article 266(1) Article 266(2) Article 267(1) Nature of Inflow All government revenues, borrowings & loan recoveries Moneys held in trust/custody (Provident funds, judicial deposits, savings bank deposits) An imprest placed at disposal of the President for unforeseen expenses Controlling Authority Parliament of India Executive / Government (operates as a banker) President of India (administered by Finance Secretary on President's behalf) Prior Parliamentary Vote Mandatory via Appropriation Act (Art. 114) NOT required (Executive disbursements) NOT required for advances (Ex-post facto approval needed later)

Feature Consolidated Fund of India (CFI) Public Account of India Contingency Fund of India Corpus / Nature Dynamic main treasury account Operational banking account Fixed statutory corpus Charged vs. Voted Expenditure on the Consolidated Fund  Charged Expenditure (Non-Votable): o Can be discussed by both Houses of Parliament, but is NOT submitted to the vote of Parliament. o Guaranteed by the Constitution to maintain the financial independence of constitutional offices.  Expenditures Specifically Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3)): o Emoluments and allowances of the President and office expenses. o Salaries, allowances, and pensions of the Chairman & Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, and Speaker & Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha. o Salaries, allowances, and pensions of Judges of the Supreme Court. o Pensions ONLY of High Court Judges (Classic    Trap). o Salary, allowances, and pensions of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG). o Debt charges for which the Government of India is liable (interest, sinking fund charges). o Any sum required to satisfy any judgment, decree, or arbitral award against the Government of India. Who is NOT Charged on the CFI?  Vice-President's Salary: The Vice-President receives NO salary as Vice-President; salary is drawn in the capacity of Chairman of Rajya Sabha (which is charged).  Prime Minister & Union Ministers: Salaries and allowances of the Prime Minister and other Ministers are VOTABLE (NOT charged).  Election Commission of India (ECI): Salaries and administrative expenses of CEC and Election Commissioners are NOT charged on the CFI (Source PYQ distinction).  High Court Judges (The Dual-Fund Trap): o Salaries & Allowances: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 202(3)). o Pensions: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3)(d)(iii)).  Governor's Emoluments: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.

Constitutional Financial Article Chain  Article 265: No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.  Article 266: Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts (Union and States).  Article 267: Contingency Fund (Union and States).  Article 112: Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget).  Article 113: Procedure in Parliament with respect to estimates (Demands for Grants).  Article 114: Appropriation Bills (Authority for withdrawal from CFI).  Article 115: Supplementary, Additional, or Excess Grants.  Article 116: Vote on Account, Votes of Credit, and Exceptional Grants.
