x: Indian State legislatures are governed under Part VI of the Constitution.
Part VI contains Articles 168 to 212 concerning Indian State legislatures.
A bicameral State legislature consists of the Governor, the Legislative Assembly, and the Legislative Council.
The Legislative Assembly is the Lower House in a bicameral State legislature.
The Legislative Council is the Upper House in a bicameral State legislature.
A unicameral State legislature consists of the Governor and the Legislative Assembly.
India currently has 6 bicameral States.
Andhra Pradesh is a bicameral State.
Telangana is a bicameral State.
Bihar is a bicameral State.
Maharashtra is a bicameral State.
Karnataka is a bicameral State.
Uttar Pradesh is a bicameral State.
Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 seats.
Bicameralism was first introduced in India at the Central level by the Government of India Act, 1919.
The Government of India Act, 1919, created the Council of State and the Central Legislative Assembly.
The State Legislative Council is also called the Vidhan Parishad.
The Council of States is also called the Rajya Sabha.
The State Legislative Assembly is also called the Vidhan Sabha.
The State Legislative Council is governed by Article 171.
The Council of States is governed by Article 80.
The State Legislative Assembly is governed by Article 170.
The State Legislative Council is a permanent body.
The State Legislative Council cannot be dissolved.
The Council of States is a permanent body.
The Council of States cannot be dissolved.
The State Legislative Assembly is temporary and dissolvable.
The normal term of the State Legislative Assembly is 5 years.
The State Legislative Council can be abolished.
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169.
The Council of States cannot be abolished.
The State Legislative Assembly can be dissolved.
The State Legislative Assembly cannot be abolished.
Members of the State Legislative Council have a 6-year term.
One-third of the members of the State Legislative Council retire every 2 years.
Members of the Council of States have a 6-year term.
One-third of the members of the Council of States retire every 2 years.
Members of the State Legislative Assembly have a 5-year term unless the Assembly is dissolved earlier.
The minimum age for membership of the State Legislative Council is 30 years.
The minimum age for membership of the Council of States is 30 years.
The minimum age for membership of the State Legislative Assembly is 25 years.
The maximum size of a State Legislative Council is one-third of the State Legislative Assembly.
The minimum size of a State Legislative Council is 40 members.
The maximum size of the Council of States is 250 members.
The maximum size of a State Legislative Assembly is 500 members.
The minimum size of a State Legislative Assembly is 60 members.
The Chairman of the State Legislative Council is elected by the Council from among its members.
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States.
The Vice-President is not a member of the Council of States.
The Speaker of the State Legislative Assembly is elected by the Assembly from among its members.
The State Legislative Assembly initiates the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council by passing a resolution.
The State Legislative Assembly resolution for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council requires a special majority.
The special majority requires at least 50 percent of the total membership of the State Legislative Assembly.
The special majority requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting in the State Legislative Assembly.
Parliament enacts the law for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council.
Parliament passes the law for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council by a simple majority.
The parliamentary law for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council is passed like an ordinary bill.
Creation or abolition of a Legislative Council is not considered an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.
The State Legislative Assembly resolution for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council is recommendatory.
The State Legislative Assembly resolution does not legally compel the Union Government to introduce a bill in Parliament.
One-third of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by local authorities.
Municipalities are among the local authorities that elect members of a State Legislative Council.
District Boards are among the local authorities that elect members of a State Legislative Council.
One-third of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by Members of the Legislative Assembly.
The MLAs elect these members from among non-MLAs.
One-twelfth of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by graduates.
The graduates electing members of a State Legislative Council must have at least 3 years of standing.
The graduates electing members of a State Legislative Council must reside in the State.
One-twelfth of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by teachers.
The teachers electing members of a State Legislative Council must have at least 3 years of standing.
The teachers must serve in educational institutions of at least secondary-school level.
One-sixth of the members of a State Legislative Council are nominated by the Governor.
Elections to a State Legislative Council use proportional representation.
Elections to a State Legislative Council use the single transferable vote system.
The single transferable vote system for State Legislative Council elections is conducted by secret ballot.
The Governor’s five nomination fields for a State Legislative Council are literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, and social service.
Literature is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council.
Science is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council.
Art is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council.
The co-operative movement is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council.
Social service is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council.
The co-operative movement is a nomination ground under Article 171 for State Legislative Councils.
The co-operative movement is not a nomination ground for the Rajya Sabha under Article 80.
Industrialists are not valid nomination categories for a State Legislative Council.
Commerce is not a valid nomination category for a State Legislative Council.
A Money Bill can originate only in the Legislative Assembly.
The Legislative Council receives a Money Bill only for recommendations.
The Legislative Council must return a Money Bill within 14 days.
The Legislative Assembly may accept or reject any recommendation of the Legislative Council on a Money Bill.
A Money Bill is deemed to have been passed upon expiry of 14 days if the Legislative Council does not return it.
The Legislative Council has no veto power over ordinary bills.
The Legislative Council cannot permanently block legislation passed by the Legislative Assembly.
The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for a maximum of 3 months after its first passage.
The Legislative Assembly can re-pass an ordinary bill after its first passage through the Legislative Council.
The Legislative Council can delay a re-passed ordinary bill for a maximum of 1 month.
The total maximum period for which the Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill is 4 months.
The 4-month maximum delay consists of 3 months after the first passage and 1 month after re-passage.
The Legislative Council cannot be dissolved on the recommendation of the Governor.
The Chairman of the Legislative Council is chosen by the Council members from among themselves under Article 182.
The Governor does not nominate the Chairman of the Legislative Council.

Bicameral Legislature & State Legislative Council  Constitutional Basis: Governed under Part VI (Articles 168–212).  State Legislature Structure (Art. 168): o Bicameral States: Governor + Legislative Assembly (Lower House) + Legislative Council (Upper House). o Unicameral States: Governor + Legislative Assembly.  Current 6 Bicameral States: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Uttar Pradesh (Largest Council: Uttar Pradesh with 100 seats).  Historical Origin: Bicameralism was first introduced in India at the Central level by the Government of India Act, 1919 (Council of State and Central Legislative Assembly). Comparison: Legislative Council vs. Rajya Sabha vs. Legislative Assembly Feature

State Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) Council of States (Rajya Sabha) State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) Constitutional Article Article 171 Article 80 Article 170 Chamber Nature Permanent Body; cannot be dissolved Permanent Body; cannot be dissolved Temporary / Dissolvable; 5-year term Abolition / Dissolution Cannot be dissolved, but CAN be abolished (Art. 169) Cannot be dissolved and CANNOT be abolished Can be dissolved, but CANNOT be abolished Member Term & Rotation 6-Year Term; 1/3rd retire every 2 years 6-Year Term; 1/3rd retire every 2 years 5-Year Term (Unless dissolved earlier) Minimum Age 30 Years 30 Years 25 Years
Feature

State Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) Council of States (Rajya Sabha) State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) Size Constraints Max: 1/3rd of Assembly | Min: 40 Max: 250 Members Max: 500 | Min: 60 Presiding Head Chairman (Elected by Council from its members) Vice-President (Ex- officio Chairman; non- member) Speaker (Elected by Assembly from its members) Creation & Abolition Mechanism (Article 169) 1. State Assembly Resolution: Initiated by the State Legislative Assembly passing a resolution by a Special Majority (≥ 50 %of total membership AND ≥ 2/3 rdof members present and voting). 2. Parliamentary Law: Enacted by Parliament by a Simple Majority (like an ordinary bill). 3. Article 368 Exclusion: The creation or abolition of a Legislative Council is NOT deemed an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. 4. Trap: The State Assembly resolution is recommendatory; it does NOT legally compel the Union Government to introduce a bill in Parliament. Composition & Electoral Quotas (Article 171(3))  Electoral Breakdown: o 1/3rd elected by Local Authorities (Municipalities, District Boards, etc.). o 1/3rd elected by the Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs) from non- MLAs. o 1/12th elected by Graduates of ≥ 3 years standing residing in the State. o 1/12th elected by Teachers of ≥ 3 years standing in educational institutions ≥secondary school level. o 1/6th nominated by the Governor.  Voting System: Elections are conducted via Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV) under secret ballot.  Governor’s Nomination Fields (5 Categories): o Literature, Science, Art, Co-operative Movement, and Social Service. o Trap: Co-operative Movement exists under Article 171 for State Councils, but is NOT a nomination ground for Rajya Sabha under Article 80. "Industrialists" or "Commerce" are NOT valid categories.

Powers over Legislation: Money Bills vs Ordinary Bills  Money Bills (Art. 198): o Can originate ONLY in the Legislative Assembly. o Council receives the bill for recommendations only and must return it within 14 days. o Assembly is free to accept or reject any recommendation; bill is deemed passed upon expiry of 14 days.  Ordinary Bills & Delaying Powers (Art. 197): o Council has no veto power and cannot permanently block legislation passed by the Assembly. o First Passage: Council can delay the bill for a maximum of 3 Months. o Second Passage (Re-passed by Assembly): Council can delay for a maximum of 1 Month. o Total Maximum Delaying Period: 4 Months (3 + 1 Months). Traps:  Dissolution vs Abolition Trap: o Statement claiming "Legislative Council can be dissolved on the recommendation of the Governor" - FALSE (It is a permanent body). o Statement claiming "Legislative Council cannot be abolished" - FALSE (Can be abolished under Art. 169).  Chairman Selection Trap: The Chairman of the Legislative Council is chosen/elected by the Council members from among themselves (Art. 182)—the Governor does NOT nominate the Chairman.

x: Citizenship is governed under Part II of the Constitution.
Part II contains Articles 5 to 11 on citizenship.
Part II primarily identifies citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
The Constitution commenced on 26 January 1950.
Parliament has exclusive constitutional power to regulate citizenship by law under Article 11.
Parliament has exclusive constitutional power to regulate the acquisition of citizenship.
Parliament has exclusive constitutional power to regulate the termination of citizenship.
The Citizenship Act was enacted in 1955.
The Citizenship Rules are made under Section 18 of the Citizenship Act.
State Legislatures have no power to make citizenship laws.
The President has no power to make citizenship laws.
The Election Commission has no power to make citizenship laws.
India provides for single citizenship.
India provides for a single domicile across its entire territory.
Single citizenship and single domicile are unitary features of India’s federal structure.
The USA has dual federal and state citizenship.
Article 5 deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
Article 5 requires domicile in India for citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
Article 5 recognizes birth in India as a basis for citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
Article 5 recognizes having either parent born in India as a basis for citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
Article 5 recognizes residence in India for at least five years before 1950 as a basis for citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
Article 6 deals with the rights of persons who migrated from Pakistan to India.
Article 6 distinguishes migration before and after the permit cut-off date.
The permit cut-off date under Article 6 was 19 July 1948.
Article 7 deals with the rights of certain migrants to Pakistan.
Article 7 covers persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947.
Article 7 covers migrants who later returned to India under a resettlement permit.
Article 8 deals with the rights of Persons of Indian Origin residing abroad.
Article 8 provides for registration as a citizen by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
Article 9 deals with the voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.
An Indian citizen who voluntarily acquires foreign citizenship automatically loses Indian citizenship under Article 9.
The automatic loss of Indian citizenship on voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship reflects the single citizenship rule.
Article 10 deals with the continuance of the rights of citizenship.
Every citizen continues to be a citizen subject to laws made by Parliament under Article 10.
Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law.

The mnemonic for the five acquisition modes is B-D-R-N-I.
Birth is a mode of acquiring citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955.

Descent covers persons born outside India to Indian citizen parents.
Descent-based citizenship follows jus sanguinis.

Naturalization is governed by Section 6 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Foreigners meeting residency criteria may be granted citizenship by naturalization.

Incorporation of territory involves India acquiring a new territory.

Pondicherry is an example of territory acquired by India through incorporation of territory.
Sikkim is an example of territory acquired by India through incorporation of territory.
The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides three modes of losing citizenship.
The three loss modes are renunciation, termination, and deprivation.
The mnemonic for the three loss modes is R-T-D.
Renunciation is a mode of losing citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Renunciation is the voluntary surrender of citizenship by an Indian national.
Termination is a mode of losing citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Termination is the automatic loss of citizenship when an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires another country’s citizenship.
Termination on voluntary acquisition of another country’s citizenship is linked to Article 9.
Deprivation is a mode of losing citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Deprivation is governed by Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
The Central Government may compulsorily terminate citizenship on grounds of fraud.
The Central Government may compulsorily terminate citizenship for disloyalty to the Constitution.
The Central Government may compulsorily terminate citizenship for unlawful trading with an enemy during war.
The Central Government may compulsorily terminate citizenship if the person is imprisoned for at least two years within five years of naturalization or registration.
In the USA, only a natural-born citizen can become President.
In India, a citizen by birth is eligible to become President of India.
In India, a naturalized citizen is eligible to become President of India.
Article 58 concerns eligibility to become President of India.
Depositing money in Indian banks does not confer Indian citizenship.
Purchasing property in India does not confer Indian citizenship.
Marrying a foreign citizen does not by itself revoke Indian citizenship.
Criticizing the government or its policies does not automatically cause loss of Indian citizenship.
The claim that a naturalized citizen can never be deprived of citizenship is false.
A naturalized citizen can be deprived of citizenship under Section 10.
Persons who were citizens of Pakistan are strictly ineligible for OCI registration.
Persons who were citizens of Bangladesh are strictly ineligible for OCI registration.
Persons whose parents belonged to Pakistan are strictly ineligible for OCI registration.
Persons whose grandparents belonged to Pakistan are strictly ineligible for OCI registration.
Persons whose parents belonged to Bangladesh are strictly ineligible for OCI registration.
Persons whose grandparents belonged to Bangladesh are strictly ineligible for OCI registration.
The OCI Cardholder provision is contained in Section 7A.
The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 was passed by the Lok Sabha on 9 December 2019.
The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 was passed by the Rajya Sabha on 11 December 2019.
The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 received Presidential Assent on 12 December 2019.
The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 applies to six non-Muslim persecuted minorities.
The six non-Muslim persecuted minorities covered by the Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 are from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan.
The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 applies to persons who entered India on or before 31 December 2014.

Citizenship & Part II  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part II (Articles 5–11); primarily identified citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950).  Exclusive Legislative Authority (Art. 11): Parliament has the exclusive constitutional power to regulate citizenship, acquisition, and termination by law (Enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955; Citizenship Rules under Section 18). o Trap: State Legislatures, the President, or the Election Commission have no power to make citizenship laws.  Single Citizenship & Single Domicile: India provides for a Single Citizenship and a single domicile across the entire territory (a unitary feature of the federal structure; unlike the USA which has dual federal and state citizenship). Constitutional Articles (Articles 5–11) Article Subject Matter & Scope Core Mechanism Article 5 Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution Domicile in India + born in India / either parent born / resident for ≥ 5 yrs prior to 1950 Article 6 Rights of persons who migrated from Pakistan to India Migration before / after the permit cut-off date (19 July 1948) Article 7 Rights of certain migrants to Pakistan Migrated after 1 March 1947 but later returned under a resettlement permit Article 8 Rights of Persons of Indian Origin (PIO) residing abroad Registered as a citizen by diplomatic/consular representative of India Article 9 Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship Any citizen voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship automatically loses Indian citizenship (Single Citizenship rule)

Article Subject Matter & Scope Core Mechanism Article 10 Continuance of the rights of citizenship Every citizen continues to be a citizen, subject to laws made by Parliament Article 11 Parliament to regulate citizenship by law Comprehensive power to enact legislation for acquisition, termination & all related matters Acquisition & Loss of Citizenship (Citizenship Act, 1955)  5 Modes of Acquisition (B-D-R-N-I): 1. Birth: Based on place of birth (Jus soli / modified criteria). 2. Descent: Born outside India to Indian citizen parents (Jus sanguinis). 3. Registration (Sec. 5): Person of Indian Origin (PIO) ordinarily resident in India for 7 years prior to applying; persons married to Indian citizens. 4. Naturalization (Sec. 6): Granted to foreigners meeting residency and character criteria. 5. Incorporation of Territory: Acquisition of a new territory by India (e.g., Goa, Pondicherry, Sikkim).  3 Modes of Loss (R-T-D): 1. Renunciation: Voluntary surrender of citizenship by an Indian national. 2. Termination: Automatic loss when an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country (Art. 9). 3. Deprivation (Sec. 10): Compulsory termination by the Central Government on grounds of fraud, disloyalty to the Constitution, unlawful trading with an enemy during war, or imprisonment for ≥ 2 years within 5 years of naturalization/registration. Traps:  Head of State / Presidential Eligibility Trap: o In the USA, only a natural-born citizen can become President. o In India, both a citizen by birth AND a naturalized citizen are eligible to become President of India (Art. 58).  What Does NOT Acquire Citizenship: o Depositing money in Indian banks / purchasing property in India - NO .  What Does NOT Cause Automatic Loss: o Marrying a foreign citizen - NO  (Does not by itself revoke citizenship). o Criticizing the government or policies - NO

 Deprivation of Naturalized Citizens: o Statement claiming "A naturalized citizen can never be deprived of citizenship" - FALSE  (Can be deprived under Section 10).  Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholder (Sec. 7A): o Persons who were citizens of Pakistan or Bangladesh (or whose parents/grandparents belonged to them) are strictly ineligible for OCI registration.  Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 (CAA) Passage Milestones: o Lok Sabha: Passed on 9 December 2019 -- Rajya Sabha: Passed on 11 December 2019 -- Presidential Assent: 12 December 2019. o Cut-off Date: Applies to 6 non-Muslim persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014.

The Constitution does not prescribe a minimum of 100 sitting days per year.

Sessions of Parliament  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V (Article 85); the President summons each House of Parliament at such time and place as they think fit.  Six-Month Rule: The maximum gap between two consecutive sessions cannot exceed 6 months (Six months shall not intervene between the last sitting in one session and the date appointed for the first sitting in the next session).  Constitutional Mandate vs Practice: o Constitution mandates that Parliament must meet at least twice a year. o The Constitution does NOT specify a fixed number of sessions (having 3 sessions—Budget, Monsoon, Winter—is a parliamentary convention). o The Constitution does NOT prescribe a minimum number of sitting days in a year. Comparison: Termination of Sittings, Sessions & Houses Procedural Action Exercising Authority Scope / Impact Constitutional / Legal Effect Adjournment Presiding Officer (Speaker / Chairman) Suspends the work in a sitting for a specified time (hours, days, or weeks) Does not affect the session; pending business remains active Adjournment Sine Die Presiding Officer (Speaker / Chairman) Terminates the sitting of the House indefinitely without naming a day for reassembly Precedes the formal prorogation of the session by the President Prorogation President of India (Art. 85(2)(a)) Terminates a session of the House (on advice of Council of Ministers) Does not affect pending bills; notices lapse unless re-introduced Dissolution President of India (Art. 85(2)(b)) Ends the very life of the Lok Sabha (Rajya Sabha is permanent) Lapses pending bills, motions, resolutions (subject to Art. 107 rules)

Imp Traps  Session Gap vs Ordinance Lifespan: o Maximum interval between two Parliamentary sessions = 6 Months (Art. 85). o Maximum validity of an Ordinance after reassembly = 6 Weeks (Art. 123). o Maximum possible lifespan of an Ordinance without approval = 6 Months + 6 Weeks.  MP Absence vs House Prorogation (Art. 101(4)): o An MP's unexcused absence of 60 days can lead to vacation of the seat. o Exclusion Rule: Calculation strictly excludes periods of Prorogation and Adjournments exceeding 4 consecutive days.

 Fixed Calendar Fallacy: Any option claiming "The Constitution mandates three sessions: Budget, Monsoon, and Winter" - FALSE  (Only the 6-month maximum gap is constitutionally mandated).  Minimum Days Trap: Any option stating "Parliament must sit for a minimum of 60/90/100 days per year" - FALSE  (No minimum days prescribed in the Constitution).  Prorogation & Advice: The President exercises prorogation on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, not at absolute personal discretion.

Constitutional, Statutory & Extra-Constitutional Bodies  Constitutional Body: An authority or institution directly established, empowered, and anchored within the text of the Constitution of India.  Statutory Body: Created by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature (e.g., NHRC, Lokpal, NGT).  Extra-Constitutional / Non-Statutory Body: Established via an Executive Order or Cabinet Resolution (e.g., NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC).  Trap: The Planning Commission (1950) and NITI Aayog (2015) are Extra-Constitutional Bodies (NOT Constitutional, NOT Statutory). Comparison: Constitutional Bodies & Article Mapping Constitutional Body / Office Governing Article Appointing Head Removal / Tenure Nuance Attorney General of India Article 76 President Holds office during pleasure of President; qualified to be an SC Judge Advocate General of the State Article 165 Governor Holds office during pleasure of Governor; qualified to be an HC Judge Comptroller & Auditor General (CAG) Article 148 President Removed on same grounds & manner as SC Judge; 6 yrs / 65 yrs State Finance Commission (SFC) Article 243-I & 243-Y Governor Constituted every 5 years to review Panchayats & Municipalities finances State Election Commission (SEC) Article 243-K & 243-ZA Governor Conducts local body polls; removed on same manner as HC Judge

Constitutional Body / Office Governing Article Appointing Head Removal / Tenure Nuance Finance Commission of India Article 280 President 5 Members (Chairman + 4); qualifications determined by Parliament by law UPSC & SPSC Article 315 UPSC: President

(Art. 243-K) Traps:  NCBC Constitutional Status (Art. 338-B): Conferred constitutional status via the 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 (Do not confuse with statutory status under the 1993 Act).  Zonal Councils vs Inter-State Council: o Zonal Councils: Statutory Bodies created under Section 15 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Home Minister is the common Chairman). o Inter-State Council: Provided for under Article 263 (Set up in May 1990 on Sarkaria Commission recommendations).  Local Bodies vs Central Commissions: o Local Body Elections: Conducted solely by the State Election Commission (Art. 243-K), NOT by the Election Commission of India. o Local Body Financial Devolution: Recommended by the State Finance Commission (Art. 243-I) to the Governor.  NHRC Trap: Options pairing NHRC with an Article are FALSE  (NHRC is a statutory body under the 1993 Act).

None of the Above (NOTA)  Definition & Objective: NOTA (None of the Above) is an electoral option provided on ballot papers and Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) enabling voters to exercise a negative vote and formally reject all contesting candidates in secret.  Judicial Origin: Directed by the Supreme Court of India in the landmark judgment PUCL v. Union of India on 27 September 2013.  Constitutional Foundation: The Supreme Court linked the right to register a negative vote in secrecy with the Freedom of Speech and Expression under Article 19(1)(a). Major Electoral Technology & Reform Milestones  1982: First experimental use of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) in the Parur Assembly constituency, Kerala.  1993: Introduction of Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC / Voter ID).  4 September 2013: VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) introduced and first used experimentally in the Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland.  27 September 2013: Supreme Court directs mandatory introduction of the NOTA button on EVMs. Direct Comparison: NOTA vs Abstention vs Right to Reject Electoral Concept Legal Mechanism Secrecy Status Impact on Election Outcome NOTA Option Voter attends polling booth and presses the NOTA button on EVM Fully Preserved (Protected under Art. 19(1)(a)) Symbolic Expression ONLY; candidate with highest valid votes among contestants is declared elected Old Rule 49-O Abstention Voter entered booth and refused to vote before Presiding Officer Violated (Recorded in Form 17-A; struck down as ultra vires) Did not affect winning tally Full "Right to Reject" Voters reject all Preserved via Re-election mandated if rejection crosses a
Electoral Concept Legal Mechanism Secrecy Status Impact on Election Outcome (International) candidates ballot/EVM threshold (>50%) (NOT applicable in India) Traps

 Automatic Invalidation Fallacy: o Statement claiming "If NOTA receives the majority/highest votes, the election is cancelled and a fresh poll is held" - FALSE o Legal Position: Under the First-Past-the-Post system, even if NOTA receives the maximum votes, the contesting candidate securing the highest number of valid votes among the candidates is declared elected.  Abstention vs. Active Participation: Exercising NOTA is NOT non-voting/abstaining; it is the active exercise of the statutory right to vote by registering a neutral/negative choice.  Rajya Sabha Elections: NOTA is NOT applicable in Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council elections (struck down by SC in 2018; limited to direct Lok Sabha & Assembly elections).

State of Kerala (1973) Article 368 (Part XX) Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution is plenary but limited; it cannot abrogate, alter, or destroy its essential foundation/basic features. Judicial Review Doctrine Marbury v. Madison (1803) (Chief Justice John Marshall, USA) Articles 13, 32, 136, 137, 226, 227 Power of the higher judiciary (SC + HCs) to adjudicate on the constitutional validity of legislative acts and executive actions. Doctrine of Severability A.K. Gopalan (1950) / State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) Article 13(1) & 13(2) Only the offending/unconstitutional portion of a statute is declared void, leaving the valid rest intact if they can be separated. Doctrine of Eclipse Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955) Article 13(1) Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are not dead ab initio, but remain overshadowed/dormant (eclipsed) and become active if the FR is amended.

Doctrine Origin Case / Landmark Authority Core Constitutional Article Foundational Legal Principle Doctrine of Pith and Substance Prafulla Kumar v. Bank of Commerce (1947) / State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla (1959) Article 246 (7th Schedule) Resolves legislative field overlaps; examines the true nature and essence of a law rather than its incidental encroachment on another List. Doctrine of Colorable Legislation Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar (1952) Article 246 "What cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly"— transgression of legislative competence masked under a permissible guise. Constitutional Amendment Battle (Art. 368 vs Part III)  Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Upheld the 1st CAA; ruled that ordinary law under Art. 13(2) does not include constitutional amendments under Art. 368 (Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights).  Golaknath (1967): Overruled earlier cases; held that an amendment is "law" under Art. 13(2) and Parliament cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right.  Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973): Delivered by the largest bench (13 Judges; 7:6 majority); held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution (including FRs), but cannot damage or destroy the "Basic Structure".  Minerva Mills (1980): Reaffirmed that a limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature; invalidated clauses (4) and (5) of Art. 368 inserted by the 42nd CAA. Imp Traps  Textual Fallacy: Statement claiming "The term 'Basic Structure' is explicitly defined in Part XX of the Constitution" - FALSE  (Judicially formulated concept).  Fundamental Rights Absolute Immunity Trap: o Statement claiming "Fundamental Rights can never be amended post- Kesavananda" - FALSE o Correct Principle: FRs can be amended, provided the amendment does not violate the Basic Structure.

 Judicial Review as Basic Structure: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), and L. Chandra Kumar (1997), Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was explicitly declared an inviolable part of the Basic Structure.  India vs UK Constitutional Model: o India: Constitutional Supremacy + Judicial Review of primary legislation. o United Kingdom: Parliamentary Sovereignty (No striking down of primary parliamentary statutes).

• Excludes Inter-State Water Disputes (Art. 262). Writ Jurisdiction Article 32 Direct enforcement of Fundamental Rights (Part III); issues Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, • SC writ scope is narrower than High Courts (Art. 226 covers FRs + legal rights).
Jurisdiction Type Governing Article(s) Core Scope & Subject Matter Note Certiorari, Quo Warranto

• SC cannot refuse an Art. 32 petition (it is itself a Fundamental Right). Appellate: Constitutional Article 132 Appeals from High Court judgments involving a substantial question of law as to interpretation of the Constitution Requires a certificate from the High Court under Article 134A. Appellate: Civil Article 133 Appeals in civil proceedings involving a substantial question of law of general importance High Court must certify under Art. 134A that the question needs SC determination. Appellate: Criminal Article 134 Appeals in criminal proceedings where HC reversed acquittal to death sentence or withdrew trial to itself Available as of right in capital punishment reversals without HC certificate. Special Leave Petition (SLP) Article 136 Discretionary appellate power to grant leave to appeal from any judgment/order of any court/tribunal Plenary & residual power; does NOT apply to Military Tribunals / Armed Forces Courts (Art. 136(2)). Review Jurisdiction Article 137 Power of Supreme Court to review its own judgments or orders Distinct from Judicial Review of statutes; subject to Parliamentary law and Court rules. Advisory Jurisdiction Article 143 President refers questions of law/fact of public importance for the Court's opinion • Art. 143(1): Public importance -- SC may tender opinion.

Jurisdiction Type Governing Article(s) Core Scope & Subject Matter Note • Art. 143(2): Pre- constitutional matters -- SC must tender opinion. Curative Petitions & Special Powers (Articles 141 & 142)  Article 141 (Binding Precedent): The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India.  Article 142 (Complete Justice): o Empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing "Complete Justice" in any cause or matter pending before it. o Operates unhindered by ordinary statutory limitations.  Curative Petition (Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra, 2002): o Evolved by the Supreme Court under its inherent powers anchored in Article 142 to prevent abuse of process and cure gross miscarriages of justice after a review petition under Article 137 has been dismissed. Benches, Courts of Record & Appointment Mechanics  Constitution Bench (Article 145(3)): o Minimum 5 Judges required to hear any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution or for references under Article 143.  Court of Record (Article 129 vs Article 215): o Supreme Court (Art. 129): Decisions have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned in subordinate courts; has inherent power to punish for contempt of itself. o High Court (Art. 215): Parallel Court of Record status at the State level.  Supreme Court Collegium Framework: o Composition: CJI + 4 Senior-most Supreme Court Judges (Total = 5 members). o Genesis: Judicially evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1st Case: 1981 -- 2nd Case: 1993 -- 3rd Case: 1998). o Trap: Neither created by an Act of Parliament nor explicitly written in the Constitution.

Imp Traps  Original Jurisdiction Exclusions (Art. 131): Inter-State water disputes (Art. 262), Finance Commission matters (Art. 280), and recovery of damages by a private party against the Union are NOT covered under Article 131.  SLP Armed Forces Exception (Art. 136(2)): Special Leave Petitions do NOT lie against judgments/sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals.  Advisory Opinion Binding Status (Art. 143): Opinions rendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 are strictly advisory and NOT binding on the President.

High Courts  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part VI, Chapter V (Articles 214–231); Article 214 mandates a High Court for each State.  Historical Origins (Indian High Courts Act, 1861): o 1862: First three High Courts established at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras. o 1866: High Court for North-Western Provinces established at Agra (shifted to Allahabad in 1869).  Strength Determination (Art. 216): The strength/number of judges for each High Court is decided and fixed by the President of India (NOT Parliament, NOT the Governor/Chief Minister). Comparison: High Court vs. Supreme Court Constitutional Parameter High Court Supreme Court Constitutional Articles Articles 214–231 (Part VI) Articles 124–147 (Part V) Strength Decided By President of India (Art. 216) Parliament by law (Art. 124(1)) Appointed By President of India by warrant (Art. 217) President of India by warrant (Art. 124) Oath Administered By Governor of the State (Art. 219) President of India (Art. 124(6)) Resignation Addressed To President of India (Art. 217(1)(a)) President of India (Art. 124(2)(a)) Retirement Age 62 Years 65 Years

Constitutional Parameter High Court Supreme Court Court of Record Article Article 215 Article 129 Writ Jurisdiction Article 226 (Fundamental Rights + Ordinary Legal Rights) Article 32 (Fundamental Rights ONLY) Advisory Jurisdiction NO ❌ (No general advisory powers) YES (Article 143) Salary & Pension Funds Salary: State Fund | Pension: Union CFI Salary & Pension: Union CFI Constitutional Article Mapping (Articles 214–231)  Article 214: High Courts for States.  Article 215: High Courts to be Courts of Record (Evidentiary value + Power to punish for contempt).  Article 216: Composition of High Courts (Chief Justice + judges appointed by President).  Article 217: Appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of a High Court.  Article 218: Application of certain provisions relating to Supreme Court (Removal) to High Courts.  Article 220: Restriction on practice after being a permanent Judge.  Article 221: Salaries, allowances, and pensions of Judges.  Article 222: Transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another by the President.  Article 223: Appointment of Acting Chief Justice.  Article 224 / 224A: Appointment of Additional/Acting Judges & attendance of retired Judges.  Article 226: Power of High Courts to issue certain Writs.  Article 227: Power of Superintendence over all courts and tribunals by the High Court.  Article 230: Extension of jurisdiction of High Courts to Union Territories.  Article 231: Establishment of a Common High Court for two or more States/UTs.

Appointment, Eligibility, Transfer & Post-Retirement Rules  Appointment Consultation Matrix (Art. 217): o Chief Justice of HC: Appointed by President after consultation with the CJI + Governor of the State. o Other HC Judges: Appointed by President after consultation with the CJI + Governor + Chief Justice of that High Court.  Qualifications (Art. 217(2)): o Citizen of India AND o Held a judicial office in India for ≥ 10 years OR o Practiced as an advocate of a High Court for ≥ 10 years o Trap: Unlike the Supreme Court (Art. 124(3)(c)), there is NO provision for appointing a "distinguished jurist" as a High Court judge.  Removal Mechanism (Art. 217(1)(b) r/w Art. 124(4)): o Removed ONLY by the President following an Address passed by each House of Parliament by a Special Majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.  Post-Retirement Practice (Art. 220): o A retired permanent HC Judge CANNOT plead/act before any court or authority in India, EXCEPT the Supreme Court and other High Courts (where they did not serve as a permanent judge). Jurisdiction: Writs (Art. 226) vs Superintendence (Art. 227)  Writ Scope (Art. 226 > Art. 32): o High Court writ jurisdiction is broader in scope than the Supreme Court because it extends to Fundamental Rights + Any other legal purpose/right. o High Court writ power is discretionary; Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.  Supervisory Jurisdiction (Art. 227): o High Court exercises administrative and judicial superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals throughout its territorial jurisdiction. o Armed Forces Exception: Does NOT extend to courts and tribunals constituted under any law relating to the Armed Forces (Art. 227(4)). Territorial Jurisdiction & Common High Courts (Arts. 230 & 231)  Parliament has the power under Article 231 to establish a Common High Court for two or more States and UTs.  Imp Cross-Jurisdictions: o Bombay High Court: Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu. o Calcutta High Court: West Bengal + Andaman & Nicobar Islands. o Kerala High Court: Kerala + Lakshadweep. o Madras High Court: Tamil Nadu + Puducherry. o Punjab & Haryana High Court: Punjab, Haryana + Chandigarh.

o Gauhati High Court: Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh. Imp Traps  Appointment Head Trap: High Court Judges are appointed by the President of India, NOT the Governor.  Oath vs Resignation Head Trap: o Oath administered by the Governor of the State (Art. 219). o Resignation submitted to the President of India (Art. 217(1)(a)).  Salary vs Pension Source Trap: o Salaries & Allowances: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State. o Pensions: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

Judges of Supreme Court vs. High Court  Constitutional Framework: o Supreme Court Judges: Governed under Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147). o High Court Judges: Governed under Part VI, Chapter V (Articles 214–231).  Appointing Authority (Universal Rule): Both Supreme Court and High Court Judges are appointed exclusively by the President of India by warrant under hand and seal (The Governor has NO power to appoint High Court Judges).  Resignation Recipient: Both Supreme Court and High Court Judges address their written resignations directly to the President of India.  Removal Mechanism: Both SC and HC Judges are removed only by an order of the President following an Address by each House of Parliament supported by a Special Majority (≥ 50 % total strength + ≥ 2/3 rd present and voting) on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Arts. 124(4) & 218). Comparison: Supreme Court Judge vs. High Court Judge Constitutional Parameter Supreme Court Judge High Court Judge Governing Article Article 124 Article 217 Appointing Authority President of India President of India (Trap: NOT Governor) Oath Administered By President of India (Art. 124(6)) Governor of the State (Art. 219) Resignation Addressed To President of India (Art. 124(2)(a)) President of India (Art. 217(1)(a)) Retirement Age 65 Years 62 Years (Raised from 60 to 62 by 15th CAA, 1963)

Constitutional Parameter Supreme Court Judge High Court Judge Distinguished Jurist Rule Eligible (Art. 124(3)(c)) NOT Eligible (No provision for distinguished jurist) Transfer Provision Not Applicable Article 222 (By President on CJI-led Collegium advice) Post-Retirement Pleading Complete Bar (Art. 124(7); no court/authority) Permitted ONLY in SC and other High Courts (Art. 220) Salary Charged On Consolidated Fund of India Consolidated Fund of the State Pension Charged On Consolidated Fund of India Consolidated Fund of India (Trap: NOT State Fund) Court of Record Article Article 129 Article 215 High Court Temporary & Acting Appointments (Articles 223–224A)  Acting Chief Justice (Art. 223): Appointed by the President from among HC Judges when the office of Chief Justice is vacant, temporarily absent, or unable to perform duties.  Additional Judges (Art. 224(1)): Appointed by the President due to temporary increase in court business or arrears of work for a period not exceeding 2 years (Cannot serve beyond 62 years of age).  Acting Judges (Art. 224(2)): Appointed by the President when a permanent Judge is temporarily absent or acting as Chief Justice (Ceases at 62 years).  Retired Judges at High Court Sittings (Art. 224A): The Chief Justice of a High Court (with President's prior consent) may request a retired HC/SC Judge to sit and act as a High Court Judge. High Court Chief Justice: Judicial vs. Administrative Capacity

 When acting in an administrative capacity (e.g., staff appointments, disciplinary actions), the Chief Justice of a High Court is subject to the writ jurisdiction (Art. 226) of another Judge of that same High Court.  The Chief Justice enjoys no absolute immunity from judicial review regarding administrative decisions. Imp Traps  The Dual-Fund Trap for High Court Judges: o Salary & Allowances: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 202(3)). o Pensions: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3)(d)(iii)).  Post-Retirement Practice Trap: o Supreme Court Judge Cannot practice in ANY court/authority in India. o High Court Judge Can practice in the Supreme Court and other High Courts (where they were not a permanent judge).  Oath vs. Resignation Head Trap: o High Court Judge's Oath Administered by Governor. o High Court Judge's Resignation Addressed to President.

State Legislatures have no power to enact laws under Article 323-A.
Parliament has exclusive power to enact laws under Article 323-A.
State Legislatures can enact tribunal laws under Article 323-B.
State Legislatures can enact Article 323-B tribunal laws on subjects within their legislative competence.
The superintendence of High Courts under Article 227 does not extend to courts constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces.
The superintendence of High Courts under Article 227 does not extend to tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces.
Article 227(4) provides the Armed Forces exception.
The Armed Forces Tribunal Act was enacted in 2007.

Tribunals  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part XIV-A (Articles 323-A & 323-B); inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.  Core Nature: Quasi-judicial, specialized dispute resolution bodies created to reduce pendency in regular courts and provide domain expertise.  Judicial Review Anchor (L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997): o The Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review of the High Courts under Article 226/227 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 is an integral part of the Basic Structure. o Clauses excluding the jurisdiction of High Courts and the Supreme Court in Articles 323-A and 323-B were declared unconstitutional. o Decisions of tribunals (like CAT) are subject to scrutiny before a Division Bench of the concerned High Court before approaching the Supreme Court. Comparison: Article 323-A vs. Article 323-B Parameter Article 323-A: Administrative Tribunals Article 323-B: Tribunals for Other Matters Scope of Disputes Exclusively covers public service matters (recruitment & conditions of service of Union, State, local/statutory authority employees) Covers a specified list of other specialized subjects (Taxation, Foreign Exchange, Industrial Disputes, Land Reforms, Ceiling on Property, Foodstuffs, Elections to Parliament/State Legislatures) Establishment Authority Created ONLY by Parliament by law (Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985) Created by both Parliament and State Legislatures (within their respective legislative competence) Hierarchy Structure Only one Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) and State Administrative Tribunals (SATs) per State / Joint A hierarchy of tribunals can be created

Key Statutory Tribunals & Appellate Matrix  Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT): o Established in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (Article 323-A). o Has original jurisdiction over service matters of civil servants under the Union. o Appeals against CAT orders lie before the Division Bench of the jurisdictional High Court (L. Chandra Kumar rule).  Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT): o Established under the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000 (Original parent act: TRAI Act, 1997). o Adjudicates disputes in telecom, broadcasting, and airport tariff matters. o Appellate Routes: Telecom/broadcasting/tariff appeals lie directly to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law; cyber appellate orders route to the High Court.  National Green Tribunal (NGT): o Statutory body established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (Guided by principles of Natural Justice, not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908). o Appeals against NGT orders lie directly to the Supreme Court (within 90 days).  Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act [IMDT Act, 1983]: o Struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) on the grounds that it violated Article 355 (Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance). Constitutional Parts Alignment Part Constitutional Subject Part IX The Panchayats (Arts. 243 to 243-O) Part IX-A The Municipalities (Arts. 243-P to 243-ZG) Part IX-B The Co-operative Societies (Arts. 243-ZH to 243-ZT) Part XIV Services under the Union and the States (Arts. 308 to 323) Part XIV-A Tribunals (Arts. 323-A & 323-B) (Inserted by 42nd CAA, 1976)

Imp Traps  Part Number Misattribution: Any option placing Tribunals in Part XI (Relations between Union and States) or Part X (Scheduled & Tribal Areas) is FALSE - It is strictly Part XIV-A.  Enactment Power Distinction (Art. 323-A vs 323-B): o State Legislatures have NO power to enact laws under Article 323-A (Vested exclusively in Parliament). o State Legislatures CAN enact tribunal laws under Article 323-B on subjects within their legislative competence.  Armed Forces Exception: High Court's superintendence under Article 227 does NOT extend to courts and tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces (Art. 227(4) / Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007).

Electronic Voting Machines (EVM)  First Experimental Use: 19 May 1982 in the Parur Assembly Constituency, Kerala (A.C. Jose v. Sivan Pillai case).  Constitutional Machinery (Art. 324): EVMs are deployed under the superintendence, direction, and control of the Election Commission of India (ECI) for Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections.  Voting Device vs. Electoral System: EVM is an electronic vote recording and counting apparatus, NOT an electoral system. India conducts direct general elections using the First-Past-the-Post (FPTP) system (where the candidate with the highest valid votes wins, irrespective of crossing 50%). Chronology: Electoral Technology & Major Reforms Technology / Electoral Landmark Year / Exact Date First Pilot / Landmark Event Legal / Administrative Context Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) 19 May 1982 Parur Assembly Constituency, Kerala Introduced experimentally; later backed by statutory amendments to the RPA, 1951 (Section 61A in 1989). Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC) 1993 Nationwide rollout initiated under CEC T.N. Seshan Established voter photo- identification to prevent bogus voting and impersonation. Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) 4 September 2013 Noksen Assembly Constituency, Nagaland Generates an independent paper slip verification visible to the voter for 7 seconds. None of the Above (NOTA) 27 September 2013 Implemented post- Supreme Court judgment PUCL v. Union of India (2013); added negative voting choice button on ballot units.

Imp Traps  The 2013 Sequencing Trap: o VVPAT was introduced first (4 September 2013). o NOTA was mandated later in the same month (27 September 2013).  First State Fully Covered by EVMs: Goa was the first State to conduct an entire General Assembly election using EVMs across all constituencies (June 1999).  First General Election Entirely on EVMs: The 14th Lok Sabha General Election (2004) was the first nationwide general election conducted entirely using EVMs.

Ordinance-Making Power  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Article 123 (President of India) and Article 213 (Governor of a State).  Nature of Power: The ordinance-making power is a legislative power of the Executive, NOT an executive or administrative function.  Core Pre-Condition: Promulgated only when the Legislature is in recess (except when both Houses are in session in a bicameral legislature, or the single House in unicameral states) and the Head of State is satisfied that circumstances exist requiring immediate action.  Co-extensive Scope: An Ordinance has the same force, effect, and limitations as an Act of Parliament / State Legislature. Comparison: President (Art. 123) vs Governor (Art. 213) Constitutional Parameter President of India (Art. 123) Governor of a State (Art. 213) Governing Article Article 123 (Part V) Article 213 (Part VI) Legislative Competence Union List (List I) + Concurrent List (List III) State List (List II) + Concurrent List (List III) Trigger Condition Either or both Houses of Parliament not in session Either or both Houses of State Legislature not in session Parliamentary / State Approval Must be approved by Parliament Must be approved by the State Legislature (Trap: NOT by President) Validity After Reassembly Ceases to operate 6 weeks from reassembly Ceases to operate 6 weeks from reassembly Prior Presidential Instruction Not Applicable Mandatory in 3 specific cases (if a Bill required prior sanction, reservation, or

Constitutional Parameter President of India (Art. 123) Governor of a State (Art. 213) Presidential assent) Withdrawal of Ordinance President can withdraw at any time Governor can withdraw at any time Scope, Powers & Limitations Matrix Operational Dimension Status Legal & Constitutional Rule Amend an Ordinary Act YES Can amend, modify, or repeal any existing Central/State legislation within competence. Retrospective Effect YES Can be given retrospective operation from an earlier date like an ordinary statute. Taxation & Budget Laws YES Can introduce or amend tax provisions within legislative power. Amend the Constitution NO Cannot be used to amend the Constitution under Article 368 (Limited to ordinary legislative power). Violate Fundamental Rights NO Subject to Article 13(2); void if it takes away or abridges Part III rights. Promulgation During Full Session NO Cannot be issued when both Houses are in active session.

The Six-Week Rule & Lifespan Calculations  Reassembly Rule: An Ordinance must be laid before Parliament/State Legislature when it reassembles and ceases to operate 6 weeks after the date of reassembly unless approved earlier.  Different Assembly Dates: If the two Houses reassemble on different dates, the 6-week countdown begins from the later of the two dates.  Maximum Lifespan: Maximum gap between sessions (6 months under Art. 85/174) + Parliamentary approval window (6 weeks) = 6 Months and 6 Weeks. Imp Traps  Withdrawal Absolute Authority: Any option stating "The President cannot repeal or withdraw an Ordinance once issued"  FALSE  (Can withdraw anytime under Art. 123(2)(b)).  Governor's Approval Source: Governor's ordinance requires approval by the State Legislature, NOT the Union Council of Ministers or the President.  Judicial Review Status: Ordinance-making power is NOT beyond judicial review (D.C. Wadhwa (1987) & Krishna Kumar Singh (2017): Re-promulgation of ordinances without legislative ratification is a subversion of the Constitution).

The Rule of Law is anchored primarily in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution.

Dicey’s first classic element of the Rule of Law is the absence of arbitrary power.

The assertion that the State has inherent unlimited police powers is false.

After Maneka Gandhi, due process of law requires freedom from procedural arbitrariness.

Uncanalized executive discretion in applying or enforcing a law directly subverts the Rule of Law.

The Rule of Law restrains the government.

Rule of Law  Philosophical Origin & Jurist: Propounded by British constitutional jurist A.V. Dicey in Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885).  Constitutional Origin / Borrowing: Borrowed from the British Constitutional System (alongside Parliamentary Government, Single Citizenship, Cabinet System, and Prerogative Writs).  Constitutional Anchor in India: Anchored primarily in Article 14 (Equality before Law and Equal Protection of the Laws), applying to both citizens and foreigners, and affirmed as part of the Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973 & Indira Nehru Gandhi, 1975). Dicey's 3 Classic Elements Operational Meaning & Legal Scope Trap / Distortion 1. Absence of Arbitrary Power (Limitation of Powers) Absolute supremacy/predominance of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power; no man can be punished except for a distinct breach of law established in ordinary legal manner. "State has inherent unlimited police powers" - FALSE 2. Equality Before the Law (Equal Subjection) Equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land administered by the ordinary law courts; no one is above the law. "Executive officials are subject only to special administrative tribunals" - FALSE (Dicey opposed French Droit Administratif) 3. Primacy of the Rights of the Individual (Liberty & Civil Rights) The Constitution is the result of the rights of individuals as defined and enforced by the courts, rather than the source of individual rights. "People's responsibility to the Government" is NOT a pillar of Rule of Law  FALSE
Core Conceptual Distinctions:

Conceptual Pair Core Difference Rule of Law vs. Rule by Law • Rule of Law: Government itself is subordinate to the law; laws must be just, fair, and non-arbitrary (Government under Law). • Rule by Law: Law is used purely as an instrument/weapon of state control to govern citizens while the ruler remains above it (Government above Law). Equality Before Law vs. Equal Protection of Laws (Art. 14) • Equality Before Law: British origin; negative concept (absence of special privilege for any individual). • Equal Protection of the Laws: American origin; positive concept (equal treatment under equal circumstances / Reasonable Classification permitted). Procedure Established by Law vs. Due Process of Law • Procedure Established by Law (Art. 21 text): Law is valid if enacted following correct legislative procedure (A.K. Gopalan, 1950). • Due Process of Law (Post-Maneka Gandhi, 1978): Law must also be "just, fair, and reasonable" and free from procedural arbitrariness. Constitutional Government • Synonymous with Limited Government—power is defined, restrained, and checked by constitutional provisions to prevent executive tyranny. Rule of Law vs. Public Interest Litigation (PIL) •  PIL promotes and strengthens access to justice for the disadvantaged, but is NOT an indispensable prerequisite for the existence of Rule of Law (Rule of Law existed prior to PIL evolution via Arts. 14, 32, and 226). Arbitrary Discretion & Article 14  A law that confers on an executive authority an unguided, uncontrolled, and uncanalized discretionary power in the matter of application or enforcement violates the principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and directly subverts the Rule of Law.
Imp Traps  Trap:

o Option Component: "People's responsibility to the government"  DELETE (Rule of Law restrains the government, not expands citizens' obedience to authority).  Dicey's Third Principle in India: o In the UK, the Constitution is the result of judicial decisions on individual rights. o In India, the Constitution is the Source of Rights (reversing Dicey's third premise while adopting the first two intact).  Administrative Discretion Rule: Executive discretion without objective standards or judicial safeguards is ultra vires Article 14.

Women's Political Representation  Local Self-Government Baseline: Women's political reservation was first constitutionally institutionalized through the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts, 1992.  Constitutional Baseline Quota: Mandates not less than one-third (≥ 1/3 rd / 33.33% reservation for women in directly elected seats and Chairperson offices across rural and urban local bodies.  106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam): Extends ≥ 1/3 rd reservation for women to the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, and the Legislative Assembly of NCT of Delhi. Comparison: Women's Reservation across Levels of Governance Level of Governance Governing Article(s) Enabling Amendment Extent of Reservation Offices Covered Panchayati Raj Institutions (Rural) Article 243D 73rd CAA, 1992 ≥ 1/3 rd of total seats & offices Direct seats (Art. 243D(3)) + Chairperson posts at all 3 tiers (Art. 243D(4)) Municipalities (Urban) Article 243T 74th CAA, 1992 ≥ 1/3 rd of total seats & offices Direct seats (Art. 243T(3)) + Chairperson posts (Art. 243T(4)) House of the People (Lok Sabha) Article 330A 106th CAA, 2023 ≥ 1/3 rd of total seats General seats + SC/ST reserved seats State Legislative Assemblies Article 332A 106th CAA, 2023 ≥ 1/3 rd of total seats General seats + SC/ST reserved seats NCT of Delhi Article 106th CAA, ≥ 1/3 rd of Direct seats + SC

Level of Governance Governing Article(s) Enabling Amendment Extent of Reservation Offices Covered Assembly 239AA(2)(ba) 2023 total seats reserved seats Upper Houses (Rajya Sabha & Vidhan Parishad) NO PROVISION

NIL (0%) Strictly excluded from the scope of 106th CAA 106th Amendment (Art. 334A)  Pre-Condition Trigger (Art. 334A): The reservation does NOT come into force immediately; it will take effect only after a delimitation exercise is conducted following the publication of the relevant figures of the first decennial Census conducted post- amendment.  Sunset Clause: Effective for an initial period of 15 years from its commencement (can be extended by Parliament by law).  Rotation of Seats: Reserved seats for women shall be rotated after every subsequent delimitation exercise as determined by parliamentary law. Panchayats & Municipalities: Sub-Articles & State Enhancements  Article 243D Breakdown (Panchayats): o Article 243D(2): Not less than 1/3rd of the total seats reserved for SCs and STs shall be reserved for women belonging to SCs/STs (Sub-reservation within quota). o Article 243D(3): Not less than 1/3rd of the total directly elected seats in every Panchayat shall be reserved for women (including SC/ST women). o Article 243D(4): Reservation of not less than 1/3rd of offices of Chairpersons at the village, intermediate, and district levels for women.  50% State-Level Quota Trap: o The constitutional baseline is strictly 1/3rd (33.33%). o States have statutory discretion to increase this quota: Bihar was the first State to grant 50% reservation for women in Panchayats (2006), followed by States like Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Himachal Pradesh.

Historical Trends & Electoral Milestones  Lowest Women Representation: 6th Lok Sabha (1977)  Only 19 women MPs elected.  17th Lok Sabha (2019): 78 women MPs elected (approx 14.36% of total strength, the highest up to that point). Imp Traps  Upper Houses Exclusion Trap: If an exam option states "The 106th Constitutional Amendment provides 33% reservation for women in Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils"  FALSE (Applies exclusively to Lok Sabha, State Assemblies, and Delhi Assembly).  Local Body Minimum Age Trap: The minimum age required to contest Panchayat/Municipality elections is 21 years (Art. 243V / 243F), NOT 25 years.  SC/ST Women Proportion Trap: Within SC/ST reserved seats, the mandatory sub-quota for SC/ST women is 1/3rd (not 50%).

Anti-Defection Law (10th Schedule)  Constitutional Insertion: Introduced via the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 (Added the 10th Schedule; amended Articles 101, 102, 190, and 191).  Key Dates: Anti-Defection Bill passed on 15 February 1985; came into force on 1 March 1985.  First Constitutional Recognition: Political parties were explicitly recognized in the Constitution for the first time through this amendment.  Pre-1985 Regional Precedent: Jammu & Kashmir enacted its own state Anti-Defection legislation earlier in 1979.  Subsequent Tightening: Strengthened by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 (deleted the 1/3rd "split" exception and capped the Council of Ministers at 15\% of the Lower House). Comparison: Trigger Conditions for Disqualification Member Category Disqualification Trigger Safe Harbor / Allowed Exceptions Party-Elected Member (MP / MLA) • Voluntarily gives up party membership (broader than formal resignation; includes conduct). • Votes or abstains contrary to the party whip without prior permission. • Prior permission obtained, or action condoned by the party within 15 days. • Merger: ≥ 2/3rd of the legislature party agrees to merge with another party. Independent Elected Member • Joins ANY political party after election. • Joining the government as an independent minister without taking party membership. Nominated Member • Joins a political party AFTER the expiry of 6 months from taking their seat. • Can join a political party WITHIN 6 months of taking their seat without attracting disqualification. Presiding Officer (Speaker / Chairman) • Joins another political party while holding or after vacating office. • Can voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair and rejoin the original party after demitting office.

Direct Comparison: Deciding Authority Disqualification Category Governing Constitutional Provisions Deciding Authority Nature of Binding Consultation Defection Disqualification 10th Schedule (Arts. 102(2) & 191(2)) Presiding Officer (Speaker / Chairman of the concerned House) Acts as a tribunal; NO consultation with ECI; subject to Judicial Review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992) General Disqualification (Union MP) Articles 102(1) & 103 President of India Mandatory & binding opinion of the Election Commission of India (ECI) General Disqualification (State MLA/MLC) Articles 191(1) & 192 Governor of the State Mandatory & binding opinion of the Election Commission of India (ECI) Merger Dynamics: The Old vs. New Threshold  Current Law: Disqualification does not apply if a member's original political party merges with another party and not less than two-thirds (2/3rd) of the legislature party members agree to the merger.  Trap: Defection protection for a 1/3rd "split" has been completely abolished. Imp Traps  Deciding Head Trap: The President or Governor has NO jurisdiction over 10th Schedule defection matters—it is decided solely by the Speaker/Chairman.  Time-Frame Myth: The 10th Schedule prescribes NO statutory time limit within which the Presiding Officer must decide a defection petition.  Nominated Member Window: Nominated members have a 6-month window to join a party; after 6 months, joining any party triggers disqualification.  "Voluntarily Giving Up Membership": An MP/MLA's conduct (e.g., publicly campaigning for an opposition party) can constitute voluntarily giving up membership even without submitting a formal letter of resignation.

Chief Election Commissioner 6 Years OR 65 Years of Age (Whichever is Statutory (EC Act, 1991 / Dual condition: tenure is capped by either 6-year service or

Constitutional Office / Judicial Body Tenure / Retirement Threshold Governing Article Note (CEC) & ECs earlier) 2023) reaching age 65. UPSC Chairman & Members 6 Years OR 65 Years of Age (Whichever is earlier) Article 316(2) Retires at 65 (Same as SC Judge / CEC). SPSC Chairman & Members 6 Years OR 62 Years of Age (Whichever is earlier) Article 316(2) Retires at 62 (Same as High Court Judge). Imp Traps  The 62 vs 65 Retirement Trap: o 62 Years: High Court Judges (Art. 217) + State PSC Members (Art. 316(2)). o 65 Years: Supreme Court Judges (Art. 124) + UPSC Members (Art. 316(2)) + CAG + CEC/ECs.  The 25 vs 30 Entry Age Trap: o 25 Years: Lower Houses  Lok Sabha + State Legislative Assembly. o 30 Years: Upper Houses  Rajya Sabha + State Legislative Council.  The 18 vs 21 Voting vs Contesting Trap: o 18 Years: Right to vote under Universal Adult Franchise (Art. 326). o 21 Years: Minimum age to contest Panchayat / Municipality elections (Arts. 243F / 243V).  The 35-Year Executive Trio: o President (Art. 58) + Vice-President (Art. 66) + Governor (Art. 157) all share the exact same minimum age qualification of 35 years.

Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG)  Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V, Chapter V (Articles 148–151).  Constitutional Identity: An independent constitutional authority designated as the Guardian of the Public Purse / Public Finance and the head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department.  Constitutional Weight: Described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the most important officer under the Constitution of India (one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system, along with SC, UPSC, and ECI).  Statutory Milestone (1971 / 1976): o CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. o 1976 Separation Reform: Departmentalization of Union accounts separated Accounting from Auditing (CAG was relieved of the responsibility of preparing Union accounts with effect from 1 March 1976; continues to compile and maintain accounts of most States). Comparison: CAG Appointment, Tenure, Removal & Post-Retirement Constitutional Parameter Rule / Mechanism Governing Article / Landmark Rule Note Appointing Authority President of India Article 148(1) Appointed by warrant under hand and seal (Trap: NOT PM, Finance Minister, or PAC). Tenure & Retirement 6 Years OR 65 Years of Age (Whichever is earlier) CAG Act, 1971 / Art. 148(3) Dual cap rule (Trap: NOT 5 years / 62 years). Removal Mechanism President of India following Parliamentary process Article 148(1) r/w Art. 124(4) Removed on the same grounds & manner as a Supreme Court Judge (Address by both Houses via Special Majority on proved misbehaviour/incapacity).

Constitutional Parameter Rule / Mechanism Governing Article / Landmark Rule Note Post- Retirement Employment Strict Complete Bar Article 148(4) Ineligible for any further office under the Government of India OR Government of any State. Salary & Service Conditions Determined by Parliament by law Article 148(3) (2nd Schedule) Cannot be varied to disadvantage after appointment. Administrative Expenses Charged on Consolidated Fund of India Article 148(6) All salaries, allowances, and pensions of CAG and staff are Charged (Non- votable).

Constitutional Article Mapping (Articles 148–151) Article Subject Matter & Scope Focus Areas Article 148 Comptroller and Auditor General of India Appointment, oath, tenure, removal, post- retirement ban, salary & charged expenses. Article 149 Duties and Powers of the CAG Auditing authority over receipts, expenditures, stores, and accounts of Union & States. Article 150 Form of Accounts of the Union and of the States Prescribed by the President on the advice of the CAG (Trap: CAG advises, President prescribes). Article 151(1) Audit Reports of the Union Submitted to the President, who causes them to be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
Article Subject Matter & Scope Focus Areas Article 151(2) Audit Reports of the States Submitted to the Governor, who causes them to be laid before the State Legislature.

Audit Scope vs. Functional Limits Matrix Function / Activity CAG Status Rule & Boundary Audit of Consolidated Fund Receipts & Outlays YES Audits all expenditure from CFI, Consolidated Fund of States & UTs with Assemblies. Audit of Contingency Fund & Public Accounts YES Audits all transactions relating to Contingency Funds and Public Accounts of Union and States. Audit of Stores, Stocks & Govt Companies YES Audits manufacturing, trading, profit/loss accounts, stores/stocks, and PSUs. Performance Audit (3Es) YES Evaluates Economy, Efficiency, and Effectiveness of government schemes and outlays. Day-to-Day Exchequer Control (Issue of Money) NO Universal Golden Trap: In India, CAG is an Auditor General, NOT a Comptroller (does not control the issue/drawal of money from the treasury, unlike the British CAG). Preparation of Union Accounts NO Relieved of Union account compilation since 1976 (handled by CGA under Ministry of Finance).

Function / Activity CAG Status Rule & Boundary Prosecution / Disallowance Power NO Has no power to disallow expenditure, enforce recovery, or initiate criminal prosecutions.  Relationship with PAC: CAG acts as the "Friend, Philosopher, and Guide" of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), attending meetings and assisting in the line-by-line examination of audit reports.  Initial Report Routing Trap: The CAG does NOT submit reports directly to the PAC or Parliament; reports are submitted strictly to the President/Governor first.  Ultimate Enforcing Authority: The ultimate constitutional responsibility for taking action on the findings in CAG reports rests with Parliament / State Legislature. Imp Traps  Report Submission Destination Trap: o Statement claiming "CAG submits audit reports directly to the Public Accounts Committee" -- FALSE  (Submitted to President/Governor under Art. 151).  Comptroller vs. Auditor Trap: o Statement claiming "CAG ensures no money is drawn from the Consolidated Fund of India without prior sanction" -- FALSE  (Audit is post-expenditure / ex-post facto).  Form of Accounts Advice Trap (Art. 150): Accounts are kept in the form prescribed by the President, upon the advice of the CAG (NOT by the CAG unilaterally).  Post-Retirement Ban: CAG cannot take up any further office under either the Central or State Governments (unlike UPSC Chairman, who cannot take another job, or judges who can head commissions).

The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act criminalizes instant Triple Talaq, also called Talaq-e-Biddat.
The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act prescribes up to 3 years of imprisonment for instant Triple Talaq.

Name of the Act Year Date of Enforcement (Commencement) Note Special Marriage Act 1954 January 1, 1955 Civil, secular marriage framework independent of religious rites. Hindu Marriage Act 1955 May 18, 1955 Codified conditions of Hindu marriage, divorce, and restitution of conjugal rights. Hindu Succession Act 1956 June 17, 1956 (Amended: Sept 9, 2005) Property inheritance rights; 2005 amendment gave equal coparcenary rights to daughters by birth. Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 July 1, 1961 Strictly penalizes giving, taking, or demanding dowry. Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act 1971 April 1, 1972 (Amended: Sept 24, 2021) Legalized abortion up to 24 weeks on specified therapeutic and vulnerable- group grounds. Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act 1994 January 1, 1996 Prohibits prenatal sex determination to stop female feticide. Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA) 2005 October 26, 2006 Civil remedies: protection orders, right to reside, and maintenance via Protection Officers. Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (PCMA) 2006 November 1, 2007 Replaced the 1929 Sarda Act; fixes minimum age at 18 (females) and 21 (males); child marriages are voidable. Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (POSH) Act 2013 December 9, 2013 Mandates Internal Complaints Committees (ICC) in workplaces with 10 or more employees.

Name of the Act Year Date of Enforcement (Commencement) Note Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019 September 19, 2018 (Retrospective effect; Royal Assent July 31, 2019) Criminalizes instant Triple Talaq (Talaq-e-Biddat) with up to 3 years of imprisonment.
